def jev_label(u, tau):
    """Argmax, or `current` whenever P(current) >= tau.

    Losing a correct warning (a current clause hidden from the check) costs
    more than keeping a proposal false alarm, so the current label can be
    given on less than a plurality. tau=None is the plain argmax.
    """
    p = u.get("p") or {}
    if tau is not None and p.get("current", 0.0) >= tau:
        return "current"
    return u.get("label")

The census a modification-target declaration is checked against, reproduced by hand outside tetel, and one surprising thing it reaches.

Applying the exclusion set `src/observe.rs` documents — `--exclude-dir=*.tetel`, `--exclude=*.evidence.jsonl`, one `--exclude` per file X whose sibling directory `X.tetel/` exists, and one exclusion per entry of `git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard --directory` — a plain `grep -rEI` over the worktree reproduces tetel's own counts exactly. For `block`: 187 files, 9,790 matched lines, 5,003,915 bytes. For `settings`: 14 files, which is the figure F19's capture reports. So both census numbers this design quotes are reachable by four shell commands with no tetel involved, and the exclusion set is what makes them stable — an unrestricted `grep -rEI` for `block` sweeps in `target/` and this memo's own rendered output and gave 261 files and 10,384 lines earlier in this session against 231 and 10,272 later, on an unchanging source tree.

The reproduction is delicate in a way worth recording. A first attempt at the same exclusions, differing only in how the shell expanded the exclude list, gave 183 files, 9,785 lines and 4,983,414 bytes — close enough to look right and wrong in all three figures. The line count is the most fragile of the three; the file count and the byte total are the ones worth quoting.

The census reads into `.git/`. `src/observe.rs` has no `.git` exclusion, so two of the fourteen files matching `settings` are reflog entries — `.git/logs/HEAD` and `.git/logs/refs/heads/tet30-prose-revised-since-proof` — which match because a commit subject in the reflog contains the word. model call can be switched off, refused for want of a key, fail in transport, time out, or come back
unreadable, and an empty array would read as a clean bill in every one of those states.

`status` is mandatory, and always one of:

| status | meaning |
|---|---|
| `off` | disabled, or this verb is not in `verify.verbs` |
| `unauthorized` | on, but nothing to call with. `detail` says which — an unset `verify.model` or a missing key |
| `queued` | a verification started for this mint. `queued_for` names it. Ask again on your next call |
| `skipped` | the verb is on, but this call had nothing to compare — a heading, a block citing no claim, a withdrawal, or a revision that left the compared text unchanged |
| `ok` | a verification completed. **`findings` is meaningful only here** |
| `unavailable` | transport failure, a non-2xx reply, or a draw that came back empty |
| `timeout` | the budget expired |
| `unparsable` | a good reply whose content was not a usable answer |

15:## The three shapes measured
23:## Result, 2026-08-10
47:## What these numbers do not establish

78:## Files

## The three shapes measured

| | calls | who decides | findings re-derivable without a model? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** `direct_eval.py` | 1 | the model, seeing claim and evidence together | no |
| **B** `extract2.py` | 2 | Python, comparing two extracted records | **yes** |
| **C** `judge_eval.py` | 3 | the model, seeing only the two extracted records | no |

## Result, 2026-08-10

15 cases (11 with a planted defect, 4 sound), 3 runs each.

| | defects caught | sound claims left alone | failed | cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **32 / 33** | **12 / 12** | 0 | **$0.0060** |
| **C** | 28 / 32 | 7 / 12 | 1 | $0.0532 |

B was measured on the earlier 14-case set: 17/30 caught, 11/12 left alone,
$0.0414. Its string-equality first draft scored 21/30 and 1/12 — several of
those "catches" were accidental, e.g. flagging `13.0M` against `13,003,879` as
a contradiction when the two agree.

**A wins on both axes at a ninth of the cost.** The pipeline hypothesis — that
extracting first and comparing second would beat one call — did not survive
measurement. C's false positives are all one failure mode: the extractor drops
a binding and the judge cannot tell a dropped binding from an absent one. It
reported *"the evidence contains no `pin` name or binding"* against evidence
whose lines 425-436 are the pin computation.

B keeps one property neither sibling has: its findings are re-derivable by
anyone holding the two extracted records, with no model in the loop.

## What these numbers do not establish

- **The case set is small and self-authored** — 15 cases, written by the same
  process that then measured against them. One (`supports-narrower-than-evidence`)
  was found mislabeled *by* the model disagreeing with it, and was split into
  `supports-narrower-tuple` and `qualifies-quantifier-unsettleable`. Others may
  be wrong in ways nothing has surfaced yet.
- **The cases are synthetic.** They imitate the shape of a tetel claim and its
  captured evidence; none was taken from a real memo.
- **Nothing here measures whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding
  round**, which is the actual cost argument. That needs the retrodiction test:
  run a verifier over each memo's claims as they stood at first render, and

The transfer holds for `fact` and is weaker for `claim`, which is the verb the design turns on by default.

`scope.rs`'s construction has two properties, and C1 carries only one across. The extent is (i) not typeable — "deliberately no flag to type one in" — and (ii) COMPLETE: `look` and `run` "record what they actually opened", so the author cannot exclude part of it either. For a claim, property (i) survives — the author cannot type the cited facts' captured output. Property (ii) does not. The captured side of the comparison is the output of the facts the author CHOSE to cite, and that choice is entirely author-controlled. tetel already treats it as unreliable: the `claim` tool description in src/mcp.rs:689 exists to warn about it — creating a claim "returns an OVERLAP REPORT: the id and shared designator(s) ... of every other fact whose extent touches the same file or command as the facts you cited, and which you did NOT cite ... read it and decide whether one of them belongs in this claim". An author with an overreaching proposition can cite only the facts consistent with it and the semantic verifier sees no disagreement — not because the sides agree, but because the disagreeing side was filtered out before the comparison. That is the author's diligence doing the work, which is precisely what C1's last sentence denies.

This is a `qualifies` and not a refutation: the construction still beats the abandoned `Domain ⊆ Extent`, where the author typed the domain outright. But the design should say which facts the comparison sees. If it is only `cites`, the independence claim must be narrowed to "cannot be made vacuous by typing, but can be narrowed by selection". If instead the comparison ran against the cited facts UNION the overlap set — facts already computed, already on disk, already surfaced at claim time — property (ii) would be restored and the transfer would be intact. That is a design choice this memo does not make.

def ask(url, model, case, timeout, max_tokens, effort):
    """One call, retried with a larger budget if reasoning ate the whole cap.

    Measured 2026-08-10: on identical input at temperature 0, reasoning length
    swings 516..2000 tokens run to run. When it reaches the cap the response
    comes back `finish_reason=length` with content of length ZERO — the model
    never reached the answer. Raising the cap on that draw is the fix; lowering
    it (an earlier version of this harness) is exactly backwards for a
    reasoning model. Cost is charged per token generated, so a bigger ceiling
    costs nothing on the runs that do not need it.
    """
    user = (f"CLAIM:\n{case['proposition']}\n\n"
            f"EVIDENCE — what was opened or run:\n" + "\n".join(f"  - {x}" for x in case["extent"]) +
            f"\n\nEVIDENCE — captured output:\n{case['output']}")
    spent, elapsed, cap = 0.0, 0.0, max_tokens
    for attempt in range(3):
        body = {"model": model,
                "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": user}],
                "temperature": 0.0, "max_tokens": cap}
        if effort != "none":
            body["reasoning"] = {"effort": effort}
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers=auth_headers())
        t0 = time.time()
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
            d = json.load(r)
        elapsed += time.time() - t0
        spent += (d.get("usage") or {}).get("cost", 0.0) or 0.0
        choice = d["choices"][0]
        content = choice["message"].get("content") or ""
        if choice.get("finish_reason") != "length" and content.strip():
            return content, elapsed, spent
        cap *= 3
    return content, elapsed, spent


def parse(s):
    m = re.search(r"\{.*\}", s, re.S)
    if not m:
        return None, ""
    try:
        d = json.loads(m.group(0))
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None, ""
    v = str(d.get("verdict", "")).strip().lower()
    return (v if v in ("supports", "refutes", "qualifies") else None), str(d.get("note", ""))

text: Two corrections to the tally, both found by the grounding pass over C21-C23 rather than by the author, and both now visible in the script's own output. First, errored draws are not excluded from anything: `retrodict.py` records an errored draw as unflagged with an `err` string, so a claim whose three draws all errored enters its population's denominator scored as a correct silence it was never asked for. Three claims are in that state — tet61 C8 in the supports-only population, tet30 C11 and tet56 C5 among the qualifies — and because each claim's draws errored together rather than one of three, no majority anywhere could have been flipped: 4 of 62 and 18 of 60 are conservative, not wrong. All observations in this workspace are taken against this state unless a later fact says otherwise.

How look/run capture the working tree and, crucially, what a grep records. worldstate.rs: every observation carries a Marker { root, state } where root is `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` resolved per-observation from the path the observation touched (canonicalized; NO_GIT outside a repo), and state hashes HEAD plus `git diff HEAD --binary`. observe.rs look_grep: (a) it passes -H unconditionally so single-file greps key on a real filename; (b) a ZERO-match grep records one NoMatch entry whose key is resolve_key(search root) and whose label is "no-match: <pattern> in <root>", with the marker resolved from the search root; (c) a grep WITH matches records one GrepMatch entry per matched file, keyed on the matched file's resolved path with label "<file> (grep: <pattern>)", and the SEARCH ROOT IS NOT RECORDED ANYWHERE in those entries — the comment says explicitly "keyed by that file's resolved path (fix 2), not by the search root or the grep command line". So for a positive-match grep, nothing captured distinguishes a repo-wide search from a single-file search that happened to match the same files. look_path records the opened file's key/label and per-file marker; run records key=cmdline, label "proc: <cmdline> (exit N)", marker from the process cwd.

What survives from an observation into a fact and its snapshot. pending.rs: PendingEntry carries kind (ObservationKind: Path | GrepMatch | NoMatch | Proc), key, label, output, world_root, world_state, captured_at. facts.rs mint(): the fold copies ONLY key, label, world_root, world_state into ExtentEntry — the kind is dropped, and a grep's pattern exists nowhere except inside the display label text ("no-match: <pattern> in <root>", "<file> (grep: <pattern>)"). Two schema-evolution precedents matter for extending this: (a) world_root is #[serde(default)] for entries minted before it existed, and an empty root is deliberately read as "comparable with nothing" — "check treats it that way rather than guessing"; (b) facts.jsonl ships in the snapshot with full extent entries (mint_windows reads the snapshot's facts.jsonl, and its doc says the Create timestamp "ships in facts.jsonl, and the snapshot copies refusals.log beside it"). Both are byte-equivalent — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` — so a prose/claim event timestamp (workspace clock) and an evidence record timestamp (whatever process wrote the record) are the same unit and the same epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What they are not is the same clock: `SystemTime::now()` reads the wall clock of the process that calls it, and nothing in either function or in the record shape ties the two processes together. Note also workspace.rs's separate `ts()` used for refusals.log, which formats the same value as a decimal string.

evidence.rs lines 128-216, the whole record shape. A Statement is {_type, subject: Vec<Subject>, predicateType, predicate}; Subject is {name, digest: DigestSet{sha256}} — one sha256, and it is of the claim proposition; Predicate is {verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, world, note, pin, timestamp}. There is no field anywhere in the record that names or digests a prose block, and RecordInput — the entire ingestion surface a reporter can fill — has no such field either. The only digest a grounding pass writes is over the proposition it was briefed on.

7:The answer, up front. The ticket survives contact with the codebase, but not in its own vocabulary — four reformulations, each argued below. First, the trigger: "any design that transplants" is as undecidable from prose as "a memo's recommendation" was for TET-28, so the trigger is an author-declared transplant record, and the refusal attaches to declarations. Second, and largest: "transcribed verbatim" cannot be a typed field on trust — a premise is refused unless its text is a verbatim substring of one observation's captured output inside the cited donor fact, which converts transcription from a request into a machine guarantee and makes TET-29 the first load-bearing use of the README's supporting-span-selection direction. Third, the refusal the ticket placed at `check` splits across three surfaces: quotation invariants refuse at the verb, completeness refuses at `render --out`, and `check` re-verifies both against the snapshot for documents that never passed through either. Fourth, a composition the ticket left open: the transplant's destination is a citation of a live modification target, so declaring a transplant forces TET-28's census at the landing site. What none of this touches — deliberately — is content: the tool never decides what counts as a premise, whether a selection is deep enough, or whether a discharge claim is true. Its entire effect is to move the violated property from "asserted by no claim at all" into the evidence ledger, where the existing grounding loop can reach it.
13:The ticket's rule as written — "any design or fix that transplants a mechanism from another site must carry a premise-inventory section" — has the same undecidable subject TET-28's ticket had. Nothing in the record model types anything as a transplant; deciding that a fix transplants means either reading the prose for tell-tale language or comparing code across two sites, and both are heuristic reads of content, the class this project has measured dead once (scope.rs's mention-detector flagged a legitimate quotation and missed both real overreaches) and has now shipped a refusal-shaped alternative to once (targets.rs, whose module doc carries the argument as implemented doctrine, not proposal). So the trigger is the same shape: the author declares a transplant as a structured record, the refusal attaches to the declaration, and the memo that transplants without declaring is not detected — it is made visible, by a section that renders its own absence and a non-coverage line that prints the blind spot. This memo does not re-litigate that reasoning; it verifies it transfers, and it does: the one disanalogy — a transplant is an act the design performs, where a modification target is a thing the design names — changes nothing about decidability, because in both cases the undecidable step is deciding from content that the memo is in the rule's scope at all.
23:Two objections were the reason this could not simply be assumed, and both were settled against the capture code rather than by preference. First, strictness: a donor comment wrapped across lines, with `//` or `*` prefixes and indentation inside it, is in fact a contiguous byte substring of a `look` capture. The plain open stores the file's bytes verbatim — no line numbers, no headers, no reflowing — and the `--lines` mode stores the selected lines re-joined with newlines, normalising CRLF endings and the trailing newline in that mode only; in both modes the relation is defined over the captured string itself, so what a memo can quote is exactly what was captured, never a third spelling. The cost is that the premise appears in the rendered section with its comment syntax intact, which the "never paraphrase" constraint treats as a feature: the reader sees the donor's clause as the donor's file spells it. Stripping the noise would require per-language comment knowledge, the exact coupling scope.rs's "Language-agnostic by construction" section exists to exclude. The two capture modes that genuinely fight containment — grep outputs, whose lines carry `lineno:` prefixes, and whole-search records, whose output is empty — make `look` of the donor file the natural donor capture, and the refusal's diagnostic should say so; the relation itself stays indifferent to observation kind. Whether the motivating premise itself clears this bar is not left to argument — the next paragraph tests it at the source. Second, soundness: a fact's output is the join of its observations' outputs, boundaries unstored, so whole-output containment would accept text straddling the seam between two captures — bytes never contiguous in anything the author saw. The fix is one serde-defaulted per-entry byte-length field on the extent entry, the same compatibility move that added kind and pattern for TET-28: boundaries become reconstructible, the relation tightens to "substring of a single observation's output", and a donor fact minted by an older build is ineligible with the same cheap remedy — look again.
37:## Where the refusals fire: verb, then render --out, then check
39:TET-28 moved its whole refusal to the verb and left render refusal-free. TET-29 cannot copy that placement wholesale, and the reason is a real disanalogy, not taste: a census either exists when the target is declared or it does not, but a premise inventory is built across time. The instrument works by transcribe-first — the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination; that confrontation is the mechanism. Refusing an undischarged premise at declaration would demand the destination-holds claim before the premise can exist, inverting the order into answer-first-transcribe-after, and pushing an author who cannot yet discharge a premise toward the quiet exit of never declaring it — the exact "refusing would make the honest case unwritable" failure the project's own discriminator names. So the refusals split by question. The verb refuses everything that is per-record and decidable at creation: a donor fact that does not exist or predates span boundaries, a premise that is not a genuine quotation, a destination that is not a live target, a discharge naming no live claim. Completeness — every premise on every live transplant discharged — is a property of the finished document, and it is refused at `render --out`: the act that writes the reviewable artifact and its snapshot, under the already-pinned policy that a rendered memo is never hand-edited. A memo with a declared-but-unexamined premise fails to come into existence rather than existing and failing; the remedy is singular; a preview render still assembles with undischarged rows marked loudly, so mid-work visibility survives. This makes TET-29 the first refusal on the render path, which is the design's most debatable departure — the alternative of letting the memo render and having only check fail it matches the ticket's letter, but it manufactures exactly the artifact the ticket exists to prevent and then depends on the author running check. Last, check re-verifies the whole shape against the shipped snapshot, both directions since tampering goes both ways, as a machine failure beside uncensused targets; containment is re-checked byte-for-byte from the facts.jsonl the snapshot already ships, so check still runs nothing and fetches nothing. Without a snapshot, transplant rows are human-owed unverifiable — the standing choice for every snapshot-dependent finding.
45:The rendered section sits beside the modification-target section and follows its conventions: labels rather than absolute keys, withdrawn records dropped, and — once the workspace has any claim — an empty section that renders as "none declared" rather than disappearing, because the hole is the finding and an absent section would make the same omission invisible. Per live transplant, the reader sees the donor fact and its extent labels, the destination target, and each premise's selected bytes verbatim in a fenced block with the discharging claim's id beside it. One shipped rule is deliberately inverted here: compose.rs refuses to inline captured output because output is unbounded, but a premise is an author-bounded selection, and inlining it is the entire point — the reader must see the donor's clause on the page, spelled the way the donor's file spells it, next to the claim that answers it, or the section degenerates into opaque pointers. Fenced blocks rather than table cells, because a premise legitimately spans lines and a markdown cell cannot carry multi-line text without escaping it, which would break the byte-fidelity the whole design is built on.

text: Testing the repair for the refutation of the block-timestamp definition. Replaying both shipped memos' prose.jsonl and, per block, comparing the timestamp of its LAST event against the EARLIEST event whose text equals its current text: for all 20 blocks of tet28 and all 12 of tet29 the two coincide — no block in either log was ever reverted to an earlier wording. So redefining the block's timestamp from "the event that set its current text" to "the earliest event whose text equals its current text" changes nothing about either memo's measured residue, while making a byte-exact revert restore the earlier timestamp. Under the old definition a revert appends a new Revise with a new timestamp and cannot lower it, because prose.jsonl is append-only and no event is ever rewritten.

text:
How sensitive a census figure is to scope and to when it is taken, measured over the same worktree four ways per symbol (counting matching lines and their raw byte length across every non-binary file, with .git/ and target/ either included or skipped, and this memo's own tet30 artifacts either included or skipped).

`render`: 529 lines / 1136689 bytes with everything; 486 / 373271 excluding tet30 only; 490 / 1075090 excluding .git+target only; 447 / 311672 excluding both.
`NON_COVERAGE`: 54 / 737911 with everything; 35 / 95637 excluding tet30; unchanged by excluding .git+target.
`Findings`: 41 / 698345 with everything; 23 / 57418 excluding tet30; unchanged by excluding .git+target.

Two things this settles. The earlier figures recorded in this workspace (render 486 lines / 373271 bytes, NON_COVERAGE 35 / 95637, Findings 23 / 57418) are reproduced exactly by the "excluding tet30 only" column, which is what the tree looked like when they were taken — before this memo and its snapshot existed. And the same symbol in the same tree yields 447, 486, 490 or 529 matching lines and 311672 to 1136689 bytes depending only on which directories are in scope and whether this memo's own artifacts are yet on disk. So a census byte figure is a property of an instrument and a moment, not of the symbol; the ordering — that `render` is far larger than `check_file`'s 5 lines — is what survives across all four scopings.

Two observations behind the attack findings.

(1) prose.rs lines 172-202, `revise`: it refuses only on an unknown block id and an empty `--why`. It never compares `new_text` to the block's existing text, and it writes `cite` straight through — so a revision that restates byte-identical text while replacing the citation list is an ordinary, unrefused act. The doc comment says why the `cite` parameter exists: without it "a paragraph created without a citation could never be given one ... which made `tetel review`'s own instruction ('mint the missing claim and cite it') unreachable for existing prose." So a citation-only revision is not merely permitted, it is the act the tool added the parameter to permit.

(2) ledger.rs lines 70-140, `split_row_cells`: it `trim()`s the whole line, un-escapes `\|` back to `|`, respects backtick spans, and `trim()`s every cell it emits. So a ledger cell round-trips a pipe but not leading or trailing whitespace, and — since a markdown row is one physical line — not an embedded newline either.

text:
Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) lib.rs lines 85-100: `check_file` builds its claim list as `ledger::import(&doc.body)` — from the parsed rendered document — and passes exactly those claims to both `checks::analyze` and `checks::analyze_ledger`. It never opens the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`. So the propositions every `proposition_digest` on record was computed over are the ledger-derived ones, and any check reusing the in-proof predicate must take its claims from `ledger::import`, not from `claims.jsonl`.

(2) Executing the attack's three constructions against tet29's real logs, under the rule as it stood and under a two-part repair. Under the old rule (block timestamp = earliest event bearing the current text; every cited claim required in proof): the baseline fix-round rewrite of P11 at 1786174700 is listed against anchor 1786174494, and all three escapes silence it — a citation-only revision adding the already-in-proof C4, a citation-only revision adding a record-less C99, and the dual (an old uncited paragraph P2 given a citation to a settled claim) all produce NOTHING LISTED. Under the repair — block timestamp = earliest event whose text AND citation list both equal the current ones, and the in-proof gate changed from "every cited claim" to "at least one cited claim, with the anchor taken over the in-proof ones" — the baseline is still listed, escape A is listed (P11, ts 1786176500, anchor 1786175367, cites C13+C4), escape B is listed (ts 1786176500, anchor 1786174494), the dual is listed (P2, ts 1786176500, anchor 1786174494), and the untouched memo still lists nothing.

Counts are occurrences, not distinct paths.

src/facts.rs lines 18-175: `ExtentEntry` has fields key, label, world_root, world_state, kind, pattern, out_len, matcher. FOUR of them already carry `#[serde(default)]` with an explicit "absence means not-recorded" reading: world_root ("`world_root` is `#[serde(default)]` for entries minted before it existed"), kind ("`None` means *not recorded*, never *some default kind*"), out_len ("`None` means *not recorded*, never *zero*"), and matcher ("`None` means *not recorded*, never *some default grammar*"). `pattern` is `#[serde(default)]` too but defaults to empty string rather than an Option. The census predicate `ExtentEntry::censuses` requires, among other conjuncts, `self.key == self.world_root` — it compares the KEY (not the label) against the world root, and its doc says "Both halves of the comparison are tool-captured: the key by `observe::search_key`, the root by `worldstate`."

src/facts.rs lines 505-575, `pub fn mint`: the fold from the pending buffer into a fact's extent is a pure field-by-field copy — `key: e.key.clone(), label: e.label.clone()` — so `mint` never computes or rewrites a label; whatever the pending entry carries is what the fact stores, and key and label are independent fields. The pin is computed over, per pending entry in order, `e.label`, `e.world_root`, `e.world_state`, `e.output`, each followed by a newline, then sha256. The pin therefore hashes the LABEL and does NOT hash the key. The comment says the pin is "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker".

src/observe.rs. `resolve_key` (lines 35-37) sets the key to `fs::canonicalize(path)` when that succeeds and the path as given otherwise — so the key is canonical-absolute by construction. `search_key` (lines 56-67) resolves a search root and, when it canonicalizes to the same directory as `world_root`, stores world_root's own spelling instead, "so it is about *which directory*, never about how either tool wrote it down". In the plain `look` path (lines ~368-405) the LABEL is a different value from the key: with no line range it is `path.to_string()` — the path exactly as the caller spelled it — and with a range it is `format!("{path} lines {a}-{end}")`. The pending entry's `output` is `shown` (the file contents or the selected range) and does not include the `==> {path} <==` header, which goes only into `printed`. `world.root` is already computed at this point, from the observed path (`worldstate::Session::new().for_path(p)`), and is stored on the same pending entry.

86:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) checks.rs lines 646-760, the in-proof predicate this design reuses verbatim. `current = sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)`; `grading_current` = records for that claim whose `proposition_digest` is empty (grandfathered: "A record with no digest at all predates the field. It is treated as grading the current text rather than dropped") or equals `current`. A claim with at least one record but none matching `current` is `out_of_proof` — a machine failure. A claim with no record at all is `ungrounded` — human-owed. The module's stated reason for digest-scoping every one of these: "Every check below asks what the evidence says about *what this claim says now*", and a red that only re-grounding could not clear was rejected as "undischargeable". The loop is defined purely over digests and record membership; no timestamp of any record is read anywhere in it.

(2) facts.rs lines 270-400, `mint_windows` — the one existing check that reasons over timestamps. It reads `FactEvent::Create` timestamps out of the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and refusal timestamps out of `refusals.log`, both written by the same workspace, and it states its own resolution limit rather than hiding it: a refusal whose second equals a mint boundary "cannot be placed on one side of it", so it "appears in both adjacent windows — the same `>=` choice the mint-time replay makes, for the same reason: showing twice is recoverable, hiding once is the incident this exists for." The struct carries `straddles_a_boundary` and report.rs prints the caveat. Its doc also states the standing form for a listing of this class: "The listing is only ever as complete as the log beneath it ... That is not a completeness claim in either direction: a verbatim listing asserts only what was recorded." And the reason it exists at grading time at all: "a line printed at a terminal works only if it is read in the moment, and a memo built on a bad fact otherwise renders and checks clean."",
109:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) brief.rs: `brief::build` returns "Every ledger claim, unconditionally — including one already grounded, and including one grounded only by ingested (attested-derived) evidence. Ingestion enrolls a claim in the independent-grounding loop; it does not excuse it, so nothing here may drop a claim from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds. A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on." The brief also withholds domain/extent, and `BriefItem` carries id, proposition and pin only.

(2) Measured over the two shipped memos' evidence logs (docs/design/tet28-*.md.evidence.jsonl and tet29-*.md.evidence.jsonl), grouping records by (claim id, proposition digest). Examples: tet28 C9 digest 7fa084e7 carries 10 records — 3 from pass 4789a6bc at t=1786132279..1786132288, 4 from pass 2a166dfe at 1786133008..1786133015, 3 from pass c1fa7b44 at 1786133955..1786133969, a span of 1690 seconds on text that never changed. tet28 C13 digest 65ec3111 was graded `qualifies` by two different passes at 1786133118 and 1786134028 — 910 seconds apart, again on unchanged text. 353:   "text": "Two existing mechanisms that an exclusion disclosure could ride on without a schema change.

(1) compose.rs `render_facts` (lines 205-275 of src/compose.rs): the rendered memo's "## Facts" table has a column "Extent (captured)" whose cell is built by mapping each extent entry to `e.label` and joining with "; ". So whatever a `look` writes into an extent entry's `label` reaches every reader of the committed memo; whatever it writes anywhere else does not.

(2) facts.rs `mint` (lines 413-437 of src/facts.rs): the pin is sha256 over a string built per pending entry from, in order, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `output`, each newline-terminated. 827:   "text": "Two observations on the pin operands.

(1) src/facts.rs lines 400-455: a fact's `pin` is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` where hash_input concatenates, for every pending entry, its label, world_root, world_state and output. So a fact pin is a hash of the observation's content, not a tree identifier: two facts minted in one checkout at one commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ.

(2) Running the installed tetel binary as `brief --json` over all five rendered memos in docs/design (tet28, tet29, tet30, tet46, tet47): 15, 14, 13, 19 and 26 claims respectively — 87 in total — and ZERO carry a `pin` in any of them. `render_json` omits the field when `Claim::pin` is None, so `find_stated_pin` yields None for every claim in every memo this project has written, including this one.",
837:   "text": "Two observations on where a tree state is and is not available.

The fact's `extent` is built by copying each pending entry's `key`, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `kind`, `pattern` and `out_len` — so the label IS the extent's label, verbatim. The pin is then `sha256:` over a string assembled by pushing, for every entry in buffer order, `label` + '\n' + `world_root` + '\n' + `world_state` + '\n' + `output` + '\n'; its own comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker". So altering an entry's label alters both the extent bytes and the pin, and both are carried in the `FactEvent::Create` this function builds and persists. A bound that adds a segment to a label therefore does change the extent and the pin on exactly the observations where it bites; what it leaves untouched is `output` (the captured bytes), `key`, `world_root` and `world_state`. Also visible here: `out_len: Some(e.output.len())` — the extent already carries a length derived from the captured output, so storing a measurement alongside an observation is not foreign to this record type.",
1483:   "text": "Two things that together make the zero-content case reachable and make a `look_path` shortfall recomputable from shipped bytes. (1) `look_path` (src/observe.rs:277-300) refuses exactly two conditions — a path that does not exist, and a directory — and then does `fs::read_to_string(p)` on whatever remains. No exclusion filtering is applied on this path at all: the only construction of `Exclusions` in the module is `Exclusions::decide(root_path)` at observe.rs:389, inside `look_grep`, and `decide` itself returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any root that is not a directory. So a tracked path under a `.tetel/` snapshot directory is opened by `look <path>` like any other file, and the four long-line ledgers are reachable. (2) `snapshot.rs`'s `SNAPSHOT_FILES` (src/snapshot.rs:71-100) is a ten-entry enumeration whose first element is `facts.jsonl`, so every fact's persisted `output` — for a `Path` entry, the complete selected text — ships beside the rendered memo. The enumeration's own comment says the list is enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that shipping a workspace file is a deliberate decision.",

1550:   "text": "Where the floor actually fires, measured over the four tracked files that hold a single line above 32768 bytes, by simulating this design's release rule (accumulate whole lines, counting the `join("\n")` separator between them, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the budget) against each file's per-line byte lengths in order.

The over-budget line is NEVER the first line of any of the four. Positions of the over-budget lines, and what a selection beginning at line 1 — which is exactly what a plain `look <path>` selects — releases:

  tet46 …/facts.jsonl — 20 lines, first line 978 B, over-budget lines at positions 11 (757177 B) and 15 (905745 B). A plain read releases 5 whole lines, 24947 B, stopping before line 6 (8029 B) because the budget is exhausted by ordinary whole lines, not because any line was over budget.
  tet30 …/facts.jsonl — 21 lines, first line 882 B, over-budget line at position 15 (574898 B). A plain read releases 2 whole lines, 11976 B.
  tet29 …/facts.jsonl — 11 lines, first line 1273 B, over-budget line at position 2 (57249 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1273 B.
  tet28 …/facts.jsonl — 10 lines, first line 1237 B, over-budget line at position 2 (34477 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1237 B.

So on all four, a plain `look <path>` returns between 1237 and 24947 bytes of whole lines and the floor does not fire. The floor fires when and only when the FIRST line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four is reachable from exactly five ranges: `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46, `--lines 15:B` on tet30, `--lines 2:B` on tet29 and `--lines 2:B` on tet28 (any B at or past that line). A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.",

1636:   "text": "`prose_after_proof` (src/checks.rs, doc comment through the function body) computes, per non-heading prose block with a non-empty current citation list: `first_proof[claim]` = the EARLIEST evidence record whose `proposition_digest` exactly equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition and whose verdict is not `Refutes` (an empty/pre-digest digest does not qualify; `Qualifies` does); `anchor` = the MAX of `first_proof` over those cited claims that have one, with an existential gate `if cited.is_empty() { continue }` skipping the block entirely when no cited claim is in proof; `block_timestamp` = the timestamp of the EARLIEST event in the block's history whose text AND cite-list BOTH equal the current ones (`min_by_key` over `filter(|(_,t,c,_)| t == cur_text && c == cur_cite)`), with that event's own `why` carried alongside. The block is listed iff `block_timestamp > anchor`. Because `first_proof` is a per-claim minimum, the anchor can only rise when a cited claim that previously had NO first proof acquires one; a later record grading a claim already in proof does not move it.",
1646:   "text": "Where a new workspace event can live, tested three ways.

(1) SCHEMA: `ProseEvent` in src/prose.rs carries `#[serde(tag = "event")]` with exactly two variants, `Create` and `Revise`. Both variants' later-added fields (`before` on Create, `cite` on Revise) use `#[serde(default)]` with comments stating "an old log replays exactly as it did" — i.e. field-level forward compatibility is established practice within a variant.

(2) READER: `workspace::read_jsonl` in src/workspace.rs treats a missing file as empty and skips blank lines, but maps ANY line's `serde_json::from_str` failure to `Err(io::Error::InvalidData)` and returns it — the whole log fails, no line is skipped.

(3) EXPERIMENT: I created a scratch workspace `tet61lab` whose prose.jsonl held one valid `{"event":"Create",...}` line followed by one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, then ran the build at this pin (`cargo run --bin tetel -- query prose --workspace tet61lab`). Output: `tetel: error querying: unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise` at line 1 column 14`, exit 1. So a build that does not know a new tag value cannot read the log AT ALL — including the pre-existing Create line. The scratch workspace was then deleted (`rm -rf`, confirmed absent) and `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.

(4) SNAPSHOT MANIFEST: `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES` in src/snapshot.rs is a `const [&str; 9]` explicitly enumerating the shipped files (facts/claims/prose/targets/transplants .jsonl, counters.json, pending.json, refusals.log, identity.json), with a doc comment saying it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." The same module's doc comment states "Because `render` is deterministic in the workspace alone, a snapshot either re-renders its memo byte-for-byte or it does not", and commits the project to "a rendered memo is never hand-edited."",
1722:   "text": "Two things that constrain how an ack's claim-digest component may be computed.

(1) src/checks.rs lines 336-368, `prose_after_proof`'s doc comment section "Two inputs, and the one that fails silently if swapped": `claims` "must be the ones `check_file` already imports from the *rendered document* (`ledger::import`), **never** the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`. Every `proposition_digest` on record was computed over a ledger-derived proposition, and the two are not the same string: rendering a claim into the ledger table (`compose::ledger_cell`) replaces embedded newlines with spaces, and importing (`ledger::split_row_cells`) trims every cell. Handed `claims.jsonl`'s propositions instead, a claim whose text has an embedded newline or edge whitespace would digest to something no record ever matches, this function would call it never in proof, and every block citing it would silently drop out of the list — with nothing red anywhere to say so." The same doc comment's "Existential, not universal" section records that requiring every citation to be in proof "was tried first and rejected".

(2) src/lib.rs lines 160-195, the call site. `findings.mint_windows = facts::mint_windows(&snapshot_dir);` sits immediately above, then the prose call, whose comment states `ledger.claims` is "deliberately used here, not the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`". The comment then defends reading prose.jsonl under `if let Ok(...)`: that silent skip is acceptable ONLY because "This is the same file `snapshot::check` already read moments ago, at the top of this function, via the identical `workspace::read_jsonl::<ProseEvent>` call inside `compose::render` -> `prose::load_all` (same path, same target type). A `prose.jsonl` that fails to parse here therefore already failed that earlier read too, and `findings.provenance` is already `Unreadable`, which `machine_check_failed` already reddens under `[provenance-drift]` — loudly, before this block runs. This `Err` arm is reachable only alongside a failure already reported elsewhere, never on its own". A test `check_a_corrupted_prose_jsonl_reddens_via_provenance_drift_not_silently` in tests/authoring_cli.rs is named as pinning that.",
1881:   "text": "`compose::render` (src/compose.rs lines 79-96) builds the memo from exactly five workspace logs: `prose::load_all`, `claims::load_all`, `targets::load_all`, `transplants::load_all` and `facts::load_all`. It reads nothing else. Since provenance drift is decided by re-rendering the snapshot and comparing bytes, only those five of the nine shipped snapshot files are drift-covered; `counters.json`, `pending.json`, `refusals.log` and `identity.json` are shipped but never re-rendered, so tampering with them is not drift. `identity.json` is one of these, and it is the file that decides whether the report calls a claim self-grounded or independently grounded. So a shipped-but-not-drift-covered snapshot file that changes what the report says is a category that already exists at this pin, with four members.",

99:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) checks.rs lines 646-760, the in-proof predicate this design reuses verbatim. `current = sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)`; `grading_current` = records for that claim whose `proposition_digest` is empty (grandfathered: "A record with no digest at all predates the field. It is treated as grading the current text rather than dropped") or equals `current`. A claim with at least one record but none matching `current` is `out_of_proof` — a machine failure. A claim with no record at all is `ungrounded` — human-owed. The module's stated reason for digest-scoping every one of these: "Every check below asks what the evidence says about *what this claim says now*", and a red that only re-grounding could not clear was rejected as "undischargeable". The loop is defined purely over digests and record membership; no timestamp of any record is read anywhere in it.

(2) facts.rs lines 270-400, `mint_windows` — the one existing check that reasons over timestamps. It reads `FactEvent::Create` timestamps out of the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and refusal timestamps out of `refusals.log`, both written by the same workspace, and it states its own resolution limit rather than hiding it: a refusal whose second equals a mint boundary "cannot be placed on one side of it", so it "appears in both adjacent windows — the same `>=` choice the mint-time replay makes, for the same reason: showing twice is recoverable, hiding once is the incident this exists for." The struct carries `straddles_a_boundary` and report.rs prints the caveat. Its doc also states the standing form for a listing of this class: "The listing is only ever as complete as the log beneath it ... That is not a completeness claim in either direction: a verbatim listing asserts only what was recorded." And the reason it exists at grading time at all: "a line printed at a terminal works only if it is read in the moment, and a memo built on a bad fact otherwise renders and checks clean."",
127:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) brief.rs: `brief::build` returns "Every ledger claim, unconditionally — including one already grounded, and including one grounded only by ingested (attested-derived) evidence. Ingestion enrolls a claim in the independent-grounding loop; it does not excuse it, so nothing here may drop a claim from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds. A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on." The brief also withholds domain/extent, and `BriefItem` carries id, proposition and pin only.

(2) Measured over the two shipped memos' evidence logs (docs/design/tet28-*.md.evidence.jsonl and tet29-*.md.evidence.jsonl), grouping records by (claim id, proposition digest). Every multi-record group shows the SAME digest graded by two or three distinct passes. tet28 was graded by 3 passes (2a166dfe…, 4789a6bc…, c1fa7b44…); tet29 by 2 (068c02e0…, c7ccb4bc…). Examples: tet28 C9 digest 7fa084e7 carries 10 records — 3 from pass 4789a6bc at t=1786132279..1786132288, 4 from pass 2a166dfe at 1786133008..1786133015, 3 from pass c1fa7b44 at 1786133955..1786133969, a span of 1690 seconds on text that never changed. tet28 C13 digest 65ec3111 was graded `qualifies` by two different passes at 1786133118 and 1786134028 — 910 seconds apart, again on unchanged text. (An earlier version of this note said 918 seconds; the captured output above is what settles it, and the difference is 910.) The one revision visible: tet29 C4 has two digests — 058ebe23 graded `qualifies` twice by pass 068c02e0 at 1786174420/22, then 1c542cfe (the rewritten wording) graded `supports` twice by pass c7ccb4bc at 1786175367/73. So: (a) one pass writes several records per claim, one per fact; (b) a later pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed, appending records with strictly later timestamps against the same digest; (c) a revised claim gets a new digest whose earliest record is the moment that wording first entered proof.",
194:   "text": "evidence.rs lines 128-216, the whole record shape. A Statement is {_type, subject: Vec<Subject>, predicateType, predicate}; Subject is {name, digest: DigestSet{sha256}} — one sha256, and it is of the claim proposition; Predicate is {verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, world, note, pin, timestamp}. There is no field anywhere in the record that names or digests a prose block, and RecordInput — the entire ingestion surface a reporter can fill — has no such field either. 369:   "text": "Two existing mechanisms that an exclusion disclosure could ride on without a schema change.

(1) compose.rs `render_facts` (lines 205-275 of src/compose.rs): the rendered memo's "## Facts" table has a column "Extent (captured)" whose cell is built by mapping each extent entry to `e.label` and joining with "; ". Its doc comment states explicitly that only the label is rendered, never the `key` (an absolute machine-local path) and never the captured output. So whatever a `look` writes into an extent entry's `label` reaches every reader of the committed memo; whatever it writes anywhere else does not.

(2) facts.rs `mint` (lines 413-437 of src/facts.rs): the pin is sha256 over a string built per pending entry from, in order, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `output`, each newline-terminated. The label is therefore already inside the pin. So a label that names the exclusion set makes two searches with different exclusion sets pin differently even when their matched output is identical.",
458:   "text": "Whole-worktree census of the symbol `look_grep`, rooted at /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel — the TET-28 census behind this design's one declared modification target.

What happened when it was taken is itself the observation. `look --grep look_grep /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel` succeeded server-side and recorded the search and its per-file hits into the pending buffer, but the agent harness refused to hand the result back, reporting "result (707,751 characters across 38 lines) exceeds maximum allowed tokens" and spilling it to a file instead. So the author of this memo never read the output of their own census; the 38 matched lines were captured, minted and are shipping in this fact's extent and in the snapshot regardless.

That is the return path and the retention path coming apart under measurement. tetel caps neither: observe.rs pushes the whole stdout into `printed` and the whole per-file output into the pending entries. The only cap in the chain was imposed downstream by the harness, on the return path only, and it fired.",

723:   "text": "Three observations folded into this fact.

(1) /Users/kolonicsmate/.claude/agents/lonic-designer.md lines 255-275 (the designer agent's stopping section, outside the tetel repo, read only). Three rules sit together: "Stop when `check` is machine-clean and no live claim is refuted or unexplained"; "Human-owed items never clear and are not failures ... 799:   "text": "Two observations on the pin operands.

(1) src/facts.rs lines 400-455: a fact's `pin` is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` where hash_input concatenates, for every pending entry, its label, world_root, world_state and output. The comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker", folding the marker in so "a fact minted against a different tree state pins differently even if its labels/output happen to coincide" — and notes the marker "is still carried separately in `extent`". So a fact pin is a hash of the observation's content, not a tree identifier: two facts minted in one checkout at one commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ.

(2) Running the installed tetel binary as `brief --json` over all five rendered memos in docs/design (tet28, tet29, tet30, tet46, tet47): 15, 14, 13, 19 and 26 claims respectively — 87 in total — and ZERO carry a `pin` in any of them. `render_json` omits the field when `Claim::pin` is None, so `find_stated_pin` yields None for every claim in every memo this project has written, including this one.",
810:   "text": "Two observations on where a tree state is and is not available.

(1) src/evidence.rs lines 548-600, the record read-back. `EvidenceRecord` is constructed from the statement with claim_id, verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, note, pin, timestamp, witnessed and proposition_digest — the predicate's `world: Vec<Marker>` field is NOT read back. 1402:   "text": "What a label change actually costs, in `facts::mint` (src/facts.rs:400-435). The fact's `extent` is built by copying each pending entry's `key`, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `kind`, `pattern` and `out_len` — so the label IS the extent's label, verbatim. The pin is then `sha256:` over a string assembled by pushing, for every entry in buffer order, `label` + '\n' + `world_root` + '\n' + `world_state` + '\n' + `output` + '\n'; its own comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker". So altering an entry's label alters both the extent bytes and the pin, and both are carried in the `FactEvent::Create` this function builds and persists. A bound that adds a segment to a label therefore does change the extent and the pin on exactly the observations where it bites; what it leaves untouched is `output` (the captured bytes), `key`, `world_root` and `world_state`. Also visible here: `out_len: Some(e.output.len())` — the extent already carries a length derived from the captured output, so storing a measurement alongside an observation is not foreign to this record type.",
1413:   "text": "Two things that together make the zero-content case reachable and make a `look_path` shortfall recomputable from shipped bytes. (1) `look_path` (src/observe.rs:277-300) refuses exactly two conditions — a path that does not exist, and a directory — and then does `fs::read_to_string(p)` on whatever remains. No exclusion filtering is applied on this path at all: the only construction of `Exclusions` in the module is `Exclusions::decide(root_path)` at observe.rs:389, inside `look_grep`, and `decide` itself returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any root that is not a directory. So a tracked path under a `.tetel/` snapshot directory is opened by `look <path>` like any other file, and the four long-line ledgers are reachable. (2) `snapshot.rs`'s `SNAPSHOT_FILES` (src/snapshot.rs:71-100) is a ten-entry enumeration whose first element is `facts.jsonl`, so every fact's persisted `output` — for a `Path` entry, the complete selected text — ships beside the rendered memo. 1479:   "text": "Where the floor actually fires, measured over the four tracked files that hold a single line above 32768 bytes, by simulating this design's release rule (accumulate whole lines, counting the `join("\n")` separator between them, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the budget) against each file's per-line byte lengths in order.

The over-budget line is NEVER the first line of any of the four. Positions of the over-budget lines, and what a selection beginning at line 1 — which is exactly what a plain `look <path>` selects — releases:

  tet46 …/facts.jsonl — 20 lines, first line 978 B, over-budget lines at positions 11 (757177 B) and 15 (905745 B). A plain read releases 5 whole lines, 24947 B, stopping before line 6 (8029 B) because the budget is exhausted by ordinary whole lines, not because any line was over budget.
  tet30 …/facts.jsonl — 21 lines, first line 882 B, over-budget line at position 15 (574898 B). A plain read releases 2 whole lines, 11976 B.
  tet29 …/facts.jsonl — 11 lines, first line 1273 B, over-budget line at position 2 (57249 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1273 B.
  tet28 …/facts.jsonl — 10 lines, first line 1237 B, over-budget line at position 2 (34477 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1237 B.

So on all four, a plain `look <path>` returns between 1237 and 24947 bytes of whole lines and the floor does not fire. The floor fires when and only when the FIRST line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four is reachable from exactly five ranges: `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46, `--lines 15:B` on tet30, `--lines 2:B` on tet29 and `--lines 2:B` on tet28 (any B at or past that line). A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.",

1582:   "text": "`prose_after_proof` (src/checks.rs, doc comment through the function body) computes, per non-heading prose block with a non-empty current citation list: `first_proof[claim]` = the EARLIEST evidence record whose `proposition_digest` exactly equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition and whose verdict is not `Refutes` (an empty/pre-digest digest does not qualify; `Qualifies` does); `anchor` = the MAX of `first_proof` over those cited claims that have one, with an existential gate `if cited.is_empty() { continue }` skipping the block entirely when no cited claim is in proof; `block_timestamp` = the timestamp of the EARLIEST event in the block's history whose text AND cite-list BOTH equal the current ones (`min_by_key` over `filter(|(_,t,c,_)| t == cur_text && c == cur_cite)`), with that event's own `why` carried alongside. The block is listed iff `block_timestamp > anchor`. Because `first_proof` is a per-claim minimum, the anchor can only rise when a cited claim that previously had NO first proof acquires one; a later record grading a claim already in proof does not move it.",
1593:   "text": "Where a new workspace event can live, tested three ways.

(1) SCHEMA: `ProseEvent` in src/prose.rs carries `#[serde(tag = "event")]` with exactly two variants, `Create` and `Revise`. Both variants' later-added fields (`before` on Create, `cite` on Revise) use `#[serde(default)]` with comments stating "an old log replays exactly as it did" — i.e. field-level forward compatibility is established practice within a variant.

(2) READER: `workspace::read_jsonl` in src/workspace.rs treats a missing file as empty and skips blank lines, but maps ANY line's `serde_json::from_str` failure to `Err(io::Error::InvalidData)` and returns it — the whole log fails, no line is skipped.

(3) EXPERIMENT: I created a scratch workspace `tet61lab` whose prose.jsonl held one valid `{"event":"Create",...}` line followed by one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, then ran the build at this pin (`cargo run --bin tetel -- query prose --workspace tet61lab`). Output: `tetel: error querying: unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise` at line 1 column 14`, exit 1. So a build that does not know a new tag value cannot read the log AT ALL — including the pre-existing Create line. The scratch workspace was then deleted (`rm -rf`, confirmed absent) and `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.

(4) SNAPSHOT MANIFEST: `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES` in src/snapshot.rs is a `const [&str; 9]` explicitly enumerating the shipped files (facts/claims/prose/targets/transplants .jsonl, counters.json, pending.json, refusals.log, identity.json), with a doc comment saying it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." The same module's doc comment states "Because `render` is deterministic in the workspace alone, a snapshot either re-renders its memo byte-for-byte or it does not", and commits the project to "a rendered memo is never hand-edited."",
1665:   "text": "Two things that constrain how an ack's claim-digest component may be computed.

(1) src/checks.rs lines 336-368, `prose_after_proof`'s doc comment section "Two inputs, and the one that fails silently if swapped": `claims` "must be the ones `check_file` already imports from the *rendered document* (`ledger::import`), **never** the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`. Every `proposition_digest` on record was computed over a ledger-derived proposition, and the two are not the same string: rendering a claim into the ledger table (`compose::ledger_cell`) replaces embedded newlines with spaces, and importing (`ledger::split_row_cells`) trims every cell. Handed `claims.jsonl`'s propositions instead, a claim whose text has an embedded newline or edge whitespace would digest to something no record ever matches, this function would call it never in proof, and every block citing it would silently drop out of the list — with nothing red anywhere to say so." The same doc comment's "Existential, not universal" section records that requiring every citation to be in proof "was tried first and rejected".

(2) src/lib.rs lines 160-195, the call site. `findings.mint_windows = facts::mint_windows(&snapshot_dir);` sits immediately above, then the prose call, whose comment states `ledger.claims` is "deliberately used here, not the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`". The comment then defends reading prose.jsonl under `if let Ok(...)`: that silent skip is acceptable ONLY because "This is the same file `snapshot::check` already read moments ago, at the top of this function, via the identical `workspace::read_jsonl::<ProseEvent>` call inside `compose::render` -> `prose::load_all` (same path, same target type). A `prose.jsonl` that fails to parse here therefore already failed that earlier read too, and `findings.provenance` is already `Unreadable`, which `machine_check_failed` already reddens under `[provenance-drift]` — loudly, before this block runs. This `Err` arm is reachable only alongside a failure already reported elsewhere, never on its own". A test `check_a_corrupted_prose_jsonl_reddens_via_provenance_drift_not_silently` in tests/authoring_cli.rs is named as pinning that.",
1805:   "text": "`compose::render` (src/compose.rs lines 79-96) builds the memo from exactly five workspace logs: `prose::load_all`, `claims::load_all`, `targets::load_all`, `transplants::load_all` and `facts::load_all`. It reads nothing else. Since provenance drift is decided by re-rendering the snapshot and comparing bytes, only those five of the nine shipped snapshot files are drift-covered; `counters.json`, `pending.json`, `refusals.log` and `identity.json` are shipped but never re-rendered, so tampering with them is not drift. `identity.json` is one of these, and it is the file that decides whether the report calls a claim self-grounded or independently grounded. So a shipped-but-not-drift-covered snapshot file that changes what the report says is a category that already exists at this pin, with four members.",

85:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) checks.rs lines 646-760, the in-proof predicate this design reuses verbatim. `current = sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)`; `grading_current` = records for that claim whose `proposition_digest` is empty (grandfathered: "A record with no digest at all predates the field. It is treated as grading the current text rather than dropped") or equals `current`. A claim with at least one record but none matching `current` is `out_of_proof` — a machine failure. A claim with no record at all is `ungrounded` — human-owed. The module's stated reason for digest-scoping every one of these: "Every check below asks what the evidence says about *what this claim says now*", and a red that only re-grounding could not clear was rejected as "undischargeable". The loop is defined purely over digests and record membership; no timestamp of any record is read anywhere in it.

(2) facts.rs lines 270-400, `mint_windows` — the one existing check that reasons over timestamps. It reads `FactEvent::Create` timestamps out of the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and refusal timestamps out of `refusals.log`, both written by the same workspace, and it states its own resolution limit rather than hiding it: a refusal whose second equals a mint boundary "cannot be placed on one side of it", so it "appears in both adjacent windows — the same `>=` choice the mint-time replay makes, for the same reason: showing twice is recoverable, hiding once is the incident this exists for." The struct carries `straddles_a_boundary` and report.rs prints the caveat. Its doc also states the standing form for a listing of this class: "The listing is only ever as complete as the log beneath it ... That is not a completeness claim in either direction: a verbatim listing asserts only what was recorded." And the reason it exists at grading time at all: "a line printed at a terminal works only if it is read in the moment, and a memo built on a bad fact otherwise renders and checks clean."",
97:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) brief.rs: `brief::build` returns "Every ledger claim, unconditionally — including one already grounded, and including one grounded only by ingested (attested-derived) evidence. Ingestion enrolls a claim in the independent-grounding loop; it does not excuse it, so nothing here may drop a claim from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds. A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on." The brief also withholds domain/extent, and `BriefItem` carries id, proposition and pin only.

(2) Measured over the two shipped memos' evidence logs (docs/design/tet28-*.md.evidence.jsonl and tet29-*.md.evidence.jsonl), grouping records by (claim id, proposition digest). Every multi-record group shows the SAME digest graded by two or three distinct passes. tet28 was graded by 3 passes (2a166dfe…, 4789a6bc…, c1fa7b44…); tet29 by 2 (068c02e0…, c7ccb4bc…). Examples: tet28 C9 digest 7fa084e7 carries 10 records — 3 from pass 4789a6bc at t=1786132279..1786132288, 4 from pass 2a166dfe at 1786133008..1786133015, 3 from pass c1fa7b44 at 1786133955..1786133969, a span of 1690 seconds on text that never changed. tet28 C13 digest 65ec3111 was graded `qualifies` by two different passes at 1786133118 and 1786134028 — 910 seconds apart, again on unchanged text. (An earlier version of this note said 918 seconds; the captured output above is what settles it, and the difference is 910.) The one revision visible: tet29 C4 has two digests — 058ebe23 graded `qualifies` twice by pass 068c02e0 at 1786174420/22, then 1c542cfe (the rewritten wording) graded `supports` twice by pass c7ccb4bc at 1786175367/73. So: (a) one pass writes several records per claim, one per fact; (b) a later pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed, appending records with strictly later timestamps against the same digest; (c) a revised claim gets a new digest whose earliest record is the moment that wording first entered proof.",
165:   "text": "evidence.rs lines 128-216, the whole record shape. A Statement is {_type, subject: Vec<Subject>, predicateType, predicate}; Subject is {name, digest: DigestSet{sha256}} — one sha256, and it is of the claim proposition; Predicate is {verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, world, note, pin, timestamp}. There is no field anywhere in the record that names or digests a prose block, and RecordInput — the entire ingestion surface a reporter can fill — has no such field either. The only digest a grounding pass writes is over the proposition it was briefed on.",
225:   "text": "How sensitive a census figure is to scope and to when it is taken, measured over the same worktree four ways per symbol (counting matching lines and their raw byte length across every non-binary file, with .git/ and target/ either included or skipped, and this memo's own tet30 artifacts either included or skipped).

`render`: 529 lines / 1136689 bytes with everything; 486 / 373271 excluding tet30 only; 490 / 1075090 excluding .git+target only; 447 / 311672 excluding both.
`NON_COVERAGE`: 54 / 737911 with everything; 35 / 95637 excluding tet30; unchanged by excluding .git+target.
`Findings`: 41 / 698345 with everything; 23 / 57418 excluding tet30; unchanged by excluding .git+target.

Two things this settles. The earlier figures recorded in this workspace (render 486 lines / 373271 bytes, NON_COVERAGE 35 / 95637, Findings 23 / 57418) are reproduced exactly by the "excluding tet30 only" column, which is what the tree looked like when they were taken — before this memo and its snapshot existed. And the same symbol in the same tree yields 447, 486, 490 or 529 matching lines and 311672 to 1136689 bytes depending only on which directories are in scope and whether this memo's own artifacts are yet on disk. So a census byte figure is a property of an instrument and a moment, not of the symbol; the ordering — that `render` is far larger than `check_file`'s 5 lines — is what survives across all four scopings.",

321:   "text": "Two existing mechanisms that an exclusion disclosure could ride on without a schema change.

(1) compose.rs `render_facts` (lines 205-275 of src/compose.rs): the rendered memo's "## Facts" table has a column "Extent (captured)" whose cell is built by mapping each extent entry to `e.label` and joining with "; ". Its doc comment states explicitly that only the label is rendered, never the `key` (an absolute machine-local path) and never the captured output. So whatever a `look` writes into an extent entry's `label` reaches every reader of the committed memo; whatever it writes anywhere else does not.

(2) facts.rs `mint` (lines 413-437 of src/facts.rs): the pin is sha256 over a string built per pending entry from, in order, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `output`, each newline-terminated. The label is therefore already inside the pin. So a label that names the exclusion set makes two searches with different exclusion sets pin differently even when their matched output is identical.",
381:   "text": "Whole-worktree census of the symbol `look_grep`, rooted at /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel — the TET-28 census behind this design's one declared modification target.

What happened when it was taken is itself the observation. `look --grep look_grep /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel` succeeded server-side and recorded the search and its per-file hits into the pending buffer, but the agent harness refused to hand the result back, reporting "result (707,751 characters across 38 lines) exceeds maximum allowed tokens" and spilling it to a file instead. So the author of this memo never read the output of their own census; the 38 matched lines were captured, minted and are shipping in this fact's extent and in the snapshot regardless.

That is the return path and the retention path coming apart under measurement. tetel caps neither: observe.rs pushes the whole stdout into `printed` and the whole per-file output into the pending entries. The only cap in the chain was imposed downstream by the harness, on the return path only, and it fired.",

This is the immutability an answer to "what happens to memos already committed" turns on: a fact minted under the old grep behaviour keeps the extent, output and pin it was minted with, and no later build can rewrite them.",

Running the release binary's `look --grep check /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel` and measuring four ways: the whole return is 884 lines (`wc -l` over the newline-stripped capture reports 883 separators); its last line is the parenthesised exclusion note, whose first colon-delimited field is `(skipped tetel's own output`; dropping that line leaves 883 matching lines; and the distinct first-colon fields of those 883 matching lines number 70, which is what `by_file.len()` computes. 1241:   "text": "What a label change actually costs, in `facts::mint` (src/facts.rs:400-435). The fact's `extent` is built by copying each pending entry's `key`, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `kind`, `pattern` and `out_len` — so the label IS the extent's label, verbatim. The pin is then `sha256:` over a string assembled by pushing, for every entry in buffer order, `label` + '\n' + `world_root` + '\n' + `world_state` + '\n' + `output` + '\n'; its own comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker". So altering an entry's label alters both the extent bytes and the pin, and both are carried in the `FactEvent::Create` this function builds and persists. A bound that adds a segment to a label therefore does change the extent and the pin on exactly the observations where it bites; what it leaves untouched is `output` (the captured bytes), `key`, `world_root` and `world_state`. Also visible here: `out_len: Some(e.output.len())` — the extent already carries a length derived from the captured output, so storing a measurement alongside an observation is not foreign to this record type.",
1253:   "text": "Two things that together make the zero-content case reachable and make a `look_path` shortfall recomputable from shipped bytes. (1) `look_path` (src/observe.rs:277-300) refuses exactly two conditions — a path that does not exist, and a directory — and then does `fs::read_to_string(p)` on whatever remains. No exclusion filtering is applied on this path at all: the only construction of `Exclusions` in the module is `Exclusions::decide(root_path)` at observe.rs:389, inside `look_grep`, and `decide` itself returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any root that is not a directory. So a tracked path under a `.tetel/` snapshot directory is opened by `look <path>` like any other file, and the four long-line ledgers are reachable. (2) `snapshot.rs`'s `SNAPSHOT_FILES` (src/snapshot.rs:71-100) is a ten-entry enumeration whose first element is `facts.jsonl`, so every fact's persisted `output` — for a `Path` entry, the complete selected text — ships beside the rendered memo. The enumeration's own comment says the list is enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that shipping a workspace file is a deliberate decision.",
1289:   "text": "Where the floor actually fires, measured over the four tracked files that hold a single line above 32768 bytes, by simulating this design's release rule (accumulate whole lines, counting the `join("\n")` separator between them, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the budget) against each file's per-line byte lengths in order.

The over-budget line is NEVER the first line of any of the four. Positions of the over-budget lines, and what a selection beginning at line 1 — which is exactly what a plain `look <path>` selects — releases:

  tet46 …/facts.jsonl — 20 lines, first line 978 B, over-budget lines at positions 11 (757177 B) and 15 (905745 B). A plain read releases 5 whole lines, 24947 B, stopping before line 6 (8029 B) because the budget is exhausted by ordinary whole lines, not because any line was over budget.
  tet30 …/facts.jsonl — 21 lines, first line 882 B, over-budget line at position 15 (574898 B). A plain read releases 2 whole lines, 11976 B.
  tet29 …/facts.jsonl — 11 lines, first line 1273 B, over-budget line at position 2 (57249 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1273 B.
  tet28 …/facts.jsonl — 10 lines, first line 1237 B, over-budget line at position 2 (34477 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1237 B.

So on all four, a plain `look <path>` returns between 1237 and 24947 bytes of whole lines and the floor does not fire. The floor fires when and only when the FIRST line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four is reachable from exactly five ranges: `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46, `--lines 15:B` on tet30, `--lines 2:B` on tet29 and `--lines 2:B` on tet28 (any B at or past that line). A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.",
