1349:   "text": "`prose_after_proof` (src/checks.rs, doc comment through the function body) computes, per non-heading prose block with a non-empty current citation list: `first_proof[claim]` = the EARLIEST evidence record whose `proposition_digest` exactly equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition and whose verdict is not `Refutes` (an empty/pre-digest digest does not qualify; `Qualifies` does); `anchor` = the MAX of `first_proof` over those cited claims that have one, with an existential gate `if cited.is_empty() { continue }` skipping the block entirely when no cited claim is in proof; `block_timestamp` = the timestamp of the EARLIEST event in the block's history whose text AND cite-list BOTH equal the current ones (`min_by_key` over `filter(|(_,t,c,_)| t == cur_text && c == cur_cite)`), with that event's own `why` carried alongside. The block is listed iff `block_timestamp > anchor`. Because `first_proof` is a per-claim minimum, the anchor can only rise when a cited claim that previously had NO first proof acquires one; a later record grading a claim already in proof does not move it.",
1361:   "text": "Where a new workspace event can live, tested three ways.

(1) SCHEMA: `ProseEvent` in src/prose.rs carries `#[serde(tag = "event")]` with exactly two variants, `Create` and `Revise`. Both variants' later-added fields (`before` on Create, `cite` on Revise) use `#[serde(default)]` with comments stating "an old log replays exactly as it did" — i.e. field-level forward compatibility is established practice within a variant.

(2) READER: `workspace::read_jsonl` in src/workspace.rs treats a missing file as empty and skips blank lines, but maps ANY line's `serde_json::from_str` failure to `Err(io::Error::InvalidData)` and returns it — the whole log fails, no line is skipped.

(3) EXPERIMENT: I created a scratch workspace `tet61lab` whose prose.jsonl held one valid `{"event":"Create",...}` line followed by one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, then ran the build at this pin (`cargo run --bin tetel -- query prose --workspace tet61lab`). Output: `tetel: error querying: unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise` at line 1 column 14`, exit 1. So a build that does not know a new tag value cannot read the log AT ALL — including the pre-existing Create line. The scratch workspace was then deleted (`rm -rf`, confirmed absent) and `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.

(4) SNAPSHOT MANIFEST: `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES` in src/snapshot.rs is a `const [&str; 9]` explicitly enumerating the shipped files (facts/claims/prose/targets/transplants .jsonl, counters.json, pending.json, refusals.log, identity.json), with a doc comment saying it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." The same module's doc comment states "Because `render` is deterministic in the workspace alone, a snapshot either re-renders its memo byte-for-byte or it does not", and commits the project to "a rendered memo is never hand-edited."",
1438:   "text": "Two things that constrain how an ack's claim-digest component may be computed.

(1) src/checks.rs lines 336-368, `prose_after_proof`'s doc comment section "Two inputs, and the one that fails silently if swapped": `claims` "must be the ones `check_file` already imports from the *rendered document* (`ledger::import`), **never** the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`. Every `proposition_digest` on record was computed over a ledger-derived proposition, and the two are not the same string: rendering a claim into the ledger table (`compose::ledger_cell`) replaces embedded newlines with spaces, and importing (`ledger::split_row_cells`) trims every cell. Handed `claims.jsonl`'s propositions instead, a claim whose text has an embedded newline or edge whitespace would digest to something no record ever matches, this function would call it never in proof, and every block citing it would silently drop out of the list — with nothing red anywhere to say so." The same doc comment's "Existential, not universal" section records that requiring every citation to be in proof "was tried first and rejected".

(2) src/lib.rs lines 160-195, the call site. `findings.mint_windows = facts::mint_windows(&snapshot_dir);` sits immediately above, then the prose call, whose comment states `ledger.claims` is "deliberately used here, not the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`". The comment then defends reading prose.jsonl under `if let Ok(...)`: that silent skip is acceptable ONLY because "This is the same file `snapshot::check` already read moments ago, at the top of this function, via the identical `workspace::read_jsonl::<ProseEvent>` call inside `compose::render` -> `prose::load_all` (same path, same target type). A `prose.jsonl` that fails to parse here therefore already failed that earlier read too, and `findings.provenance` is already `Unreadable`, which `machine_check_failed` already reddens under `[provenance-drift]` — loudly, before this block runs. This `Err` arm is reachable only alongside a failure already reported elsewhere, never on its own". A test `check_a_corrupted_prose_jsonl_reddens_via_provenance_drift_not_silently` in tests/authoring_cli.rs is named as pinning that.",
1537:   "text": "`compose::render` (src/compose.rs lines 79-96) builds the memo from exactly five workspace logs: `prose::load_all`, `claims::load_all`, `targets::load_all`, `transplants::load_all` and `facts::load_all`. It reads nothing else. Since provenance drift is decided by re-rendering the snapshot and comparing bytes, only those five of the nine shipped snapshot files are drift-covered; `counters.json`, `pending.json`, `refusals.log` and `identity.json` are shipped but never re-rendered, so tampering with them is not drift. `identity.json` is one of these, and it is the file that decides whether the report calls a claim self-grounded or independently grounded. So a shipped-but-not-drift-covered snapshot file that changes what the report says is a category that already exists at this pin, with four members.",

10:   "text": "Design pin: tetel repo HEAD at e19a4694bedd1bd2bda91626362f9c2d05f35274, 2026-08-08, "transplant: select the donor's premises, and answer each one". All facts in this workspace are taken against this tree unless a later fact says otherwise.",
85:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) checks.rs lines 646-760, the in-proof predicate this design reuses verbatim. `current = sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)`; `grading_current` = records for that claim whose `proposition_digest` is empty (grandfathered: "A record with no digest at all predates the field. It is treated as grading the current text rather than dropped") or equals `current`. A claim with at least one record but none matching `current` is `out_of_proof` — a machine failure. A claim with no record at all is `ungrounded` — human-owed. The module's stated reason for digest-scoping every one of these: "Every check below asks what the evidence says about *what this claim says now*", and a red that only re-grounding could not clear was rejected as "undischargeable". The loop is defined purely over digests and record membership; no timestamp of any record is read anywhere in it.

(2) facts.rs lines 270-400, `mint_windows` — the one existing check that reasons over timestamps. It reads `FactEvent::Create` timestamps out of the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and refusal timestamps out of `refusals.log`, both written by the same workspace, and it states its own resolution limit rather than hiding it: a refusal whose second equals a mint boundary "cannot be placed on one side of it", so it "appears in both adjacent windows — the same `>=` choice the mint-time replay makes, for the same reason: showing twice is recoverable, hiding once is the incident this exists for." The struct carries `straddles_a_boundary` and report.rs prints the caveat. Its doc also states the standing form for a listing of this class: "The listing is only ever as complete as the log beneath it ... That is not a completeness claim in either direction: a verbatim listing asserts only what was recorded." And the reason it exists at grading time at all: "a line printed at a terminal works only if it is read in the moment, and a memo built on a bad fact otherwise renders and checks clean."",
97:   "text": "Two observations, folded into one mint.

(1) brief.rs: `brief::build` returns "Every ledger claim, unconditionally — including one already grounded, and including one grounded only by ingested (attested-derived) evidence. Ingestion enrolls a claim in the independent-grounding loop; it does not excuse it, so nothing here may drop a claim from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds. A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on." The brief also withholds domain/extent, and `BriefItem` carries id, proposition and pin only.

(2) Measured over the two shipped memos' evidence logs (docs/design/tet28-*.md.evidence.jsonl and tet29-*.md.evidence.jsonl), grouping records by (claim id, proposition digest). Every multi-record group shows the SAME digest graded by two or three distinct passes. tet28 was graded by 3 passes (2a166dfe…, 4789a6bc…, c1fa7b44…); tet29 by 2 (068c02e0…, c7ccb4bc…). 1332:   "text": "What a label change actually costs, in `facts::mint` (src/facts.rs:400-435). The fact's `extent` is built by copying each pending entry's `key`, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `kind`, `pattern` and `out_len` — so the label IS the extent's label, verbatim. The pin is then `sha256:` over a string assembled by pushing, for every entry in buffer order, `label` + '\n' + `world_root` + '\n' + `world_state` + '\n' + `output` + '\n'; its own comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker". So altering an entry's label alters both the extent bytes and the pin, and both are carried in the `FactEvent::Create` this function builds and persists. A bound that adds a segment to a label therefore does change the extent and the pin on exactly the observations where it bites; what it leaves untouched is `output` (the captured bytes), `key`, `world_root` and `world_state`. Also visible here: `out_len: Some(e.output.len())` — the extent already carries a length derived from the captured output, so storing a measurement alongside an observation is not foreign to this record type.",
1361:   "text": "Two things that together make the zero-content case reachable and make a `look_path` shortfall recomputable from shipped bytes. (1) `look_path` (src/observe.rs:277-300) refuses exactly two conditions — a path that does not exist, and a directory — and then does `fs::read_to_string(p)` on whatever remains. No exclusion filtering is applied on this path at all: the only construction of `Exclusions` in the module is `Exclusions::decide(root_path)` at observe.rs:389, inside `look_grep`, and `decide` itself returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any root that is not a directory. So a tracked path under a `.tetel/` snapshot directory is opened by `look <path>` like any other file, and the four long-line ledgers are reachable. (2) `snapshot.rs`'s `SNAPSHOT_FILES` (src/snapshot.rs:71-100) is a ten-entry enumeration whose first element is `facts.jsonl`, so every fact's persisted `output` — for a `Path` entry, the complete selected text — ships beside the rendered memo. The enumeration's own comment says the list is enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that shipping a workspace file is a deliberate decision.",
1397:   "text": "Where the floor actually fires, measured over the four tracked files that hold a single line above 32768 bytes, by simulating this design's release rule (accumulate whole lines, counting the `join("\n")` separator between them, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the budget) against each file's per-line byte lengths in order.

The over-budget line is NEVER the first line of any of the four. Positions of the over-budget lines, and what a selection beginning at line 1 — which is exactly what a plain `look <path>` selects — releases:

  tet46 …/facts.jsonl — 20 lines, first line 978 B, over-budget lines at positions 11 (757177 B) and 15 (905745 B). A plain read releases 5 whole lines, 24947 B, stopping before line 6 (8029 B) because the budget is exhausted by ordinary whole lines, not because any line was over budget.
  tet30 …/facts.jsonl — 21 lines, first line 882 B, over-budget line at position 15 (574898 B). A plain read releases 2 whole lines, 11976 B.
  tet29 …/facts.jsonl — 11 lines, first line 1273 B, over-budget line at position 2 (57249 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1273 B.
  tet28 …/facts.jsonl — 10 lines, first line 1237 B, over-budget line at position 2 (34477 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1237 B.

So on all four, a plain `look <path>` returns between 1237 and 24947 bytes of whole lines and the floor does not fire. The floor fires when and only when the FIRST line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four is reachable from exactly five ranges: `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46, `--lines 15:B` on tet30, `--lines 2:B` on tet29 and `--lines 2:B` on tet28 (any B at or past that line). A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.",

1474:   "text": "`prose_after_proof` (src/checks.rs, doc comment through the function body) computes, per non-heading prose block with a non-empty current citation list: `first_proof[claim]` = the EARLIEST evidence record whose `proposition_digest` exactly equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition and whose verdict is not `Refutes` (an empty/pre-digest digest does not qualify; `Qualifies` does); `anchor` = the MAX of `first_proof` over those cited claims that have one, with an existential gate `if cited.is_empty() { continue }` skipping the block entirely when no cited claim is in proof; `block_timestamp` = the timestamp of the EARLIEST event in the block's history whose text AND cite-list BOTH equal the current ones (`min_by_key` over `filter(|(_,t,c,_)| t == cur_text && c == cur_cite)`), with that event's own `why` carried alongside. The block is listed iff `block_timestamp > anchor`. Because `first_proof` is a per-claim minimum, the anchor can only rise when a cited claim that previously had NO first proof acquires one; a later record grading a claim already in proof does not move it.",
1486:   "text": "Where a new workspace event can live, tested three ways.

(1) SCHEMA: `ProseEvent` in src/prose.rs carries `#[serde(tag = "event")]` with exactly two variants, `Create` and `Revise`. Both variants' later-added fields (`before` on Create, `cite` on Revise) use `#[serde(default)]` with comments stating "an old log replays exactly as it did" — i.e. field-level forward compatibility is established practice within a variant.

(2) READER: `workspace::read_jsonl` in src/workspace.rs treats a missing file as empty and skips blank lines, but maps ANY line's `serde_json::from_str` failure to `Err(io::Error::InvalidData)` and returns it — the whole log fails, no line is skipped.

(3) EXPERIMENT: I created a scratch workspace `tet61lab` whose prose.jsonl held one valid `{"event":"Create",...}` line followed by one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, then ran the build at this pin (`cargo run --bin tetel -- query prose --workspace tet61lab`). Output: `tetel: error querying: unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise` at line 1 column 14`, exit 1. So a build that does not know a new tag value cannot read the log AT ALL — including the pre-existing Create line. The scratch workspace was then deleted (`rm -rf`, confirmed absent) and `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.

(4) SNAPSHOT MANIFEST: `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES` in src/snapshot.rs is a `const [&str; 9]` explicitly enumerating the shipped files (facts/claims/prose/targets/transplants .jsonl, counters.json, pending.json, refusals.log, identity.json), with a doc comment saying it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." A claim with no record at all is `ungrounded` — human-owed. The module's stated reason for digest-scoping every one of these: "Every check below asks what the evidence says about *what this claim says now*", and a red that only re-grounding could not clear was rejected as "undischargeable". The loop is defined purely over digests and record membership; no timestamp of any record is read anywhere in it.

(2) facts.rs lines 270-400, `mint_windows` — the one existing check that reasons over timestamps. It reads `FactEvent::Create` timestamps out of the snapshot's `facts.jsonl` and refusal timestamps out of `refusals.log`, both written by the same workspace, and it states its own resolution limit rather than hiding it: a refusal whose second equals a mint boundary "cannot be placed on one side of it", so it "appears in both adjacent windows — the same `>=` choice the mint-time replay makes, for the same reason: showing twice is recoverable, hiding once is the incident this exists for." The struct carries `straddles_a_boundary` and report.rs prints the caveat. Its doc also states the standing form for a listing of this class: "The listing is only ever as complete as the log beneath it ... That is not a completeness claim in either direction: a verbatim listing asserts only what was recorded." 345:   "text": "Two existing mechanisms that an exclusion disclosure could ride on without a schema change.

(1) compose.rs `render_facts` (lines 205-275 of src/compose.rs): the rendered memo's "## Facts" table has a column "Extent (captured)" whose cell is built by mapping each extent entry to `e.label` and joining with "; ". So whatever a `look` writes into an extent entry's `label` reaches every reader of the committed memo; whatever it writes anywhere else does not.

(2) facts.rs `mint` (lines 413-437 of src/facts.rs): the pin is sha256 over a string built per pending entry from, in order, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `output`, each newline-terminated. Running the release binary's `look --grep check /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel` and measuring four ways: the whole return is 884 lines (`wc -l` over the newline-stripped capture reports 883 separators); its last line is the parenthesised exclusion note, whose first colon-delimited field is `(skipped tetel's own output`; dropping that line leaves 883 matching lines; and the distinct first-colon fields of those 883 matching lines number 70, which is what `by_file.len()` computes. Counting distinct first-colon fields over the WHOLE return — the method used for the earlier figure — yields 71, because the exclusion-note line contributes a spurious 71st field. So this census is 70 files and 883 matching lines, and 71 was an artefact of counting the note line as a file.",
1319:   "text": "What a label change actually costs, in `facts::mint` (src/facts.rs:400-435). The fact's `extent` is built by copying each pending entry's `key`, `label`, `world_root`, `world_state`, `kind`, `pattern` and `out_len` — so the label IS the extent's label, verbatim. The pin is then `sha256:` over a string assembled by pushing, for every entry in buffer order, `label` + '\n' + `world_root` + '\n' + `world_state` + '\n' + `output` + '\n'; its own comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker". So altering an entry's label alters both the extent bytes and the pin, and both are carried in the `FactEvent::Create` this function builds and persists. A bound that adds a segment to a label therefore does change the extent and the pin on exactly the observations where it bites; what it leaves untouched is `output` (the captured bytes), `key`, `world_root` and `world_state`. Also visible here: `out_len: Some(e.output.len())` — the extent already carries a length derived from the captured output, so storing a measurement alongside an observation is not foreign to this record type.",
1343:   "text": "Two things that together make the zero-content case reachable and make a `look_path` shortfall recomputable from shipped bytes. (1) `look_path` (src/observe.rs:277-300) refuses exactly two conditions — a path that does not exist, and a directory — and then does `fs::read_to_string(p)` on whatever remains. No exclusion filtering is applied on this path at all: the only construction of `Exclusions` in the module is `Exclusions::decide(root_path)` at observe.rs:389, inside `look_grep`, and `decide` itself returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any root that is not a directory. So a tracked path under a `.tetel/` snapshot directory is opened by `look <path>` like any other file, and the four long-line ledgers are reachable. (2) `snapshot.rs`'s `SNAPSHOT_FILES` (src/snapshot.rs:71-100) is a ten-entry enumeration whose first element is `facts.jsonl`, so every fact's persisted `output` — for a `Path` entry, the complete selected text — ships beside the rendered memo. The enumeration's own comment says the list is enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that shipping a workspace file is a deliberate decision.",
1376:   "text": "Where the floor actually fires, measured over the four tracked files that hold a single line above 32768 bytes, by simulating this design's release rule (accumulate whole lines, counting the `join("\n")` separator between them, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the budget) against each file's per-line byte lengths in order.

The over-budget line is NEVER the first line of any of the four. Positions of the over-budget lines, and what a selection beginning at line 1 — which is exactly what a plain `look <path>` selects — releases:

  tet46 …/facts.jsonl — 20 lines, first line 978 B, over-budget lines at positions 11 (757177 B) and 15 (905745 B). A plain read releases 5 whole lines, 24947 B, stopping before line 6 (8029 B) because the budget is exhausted by ordinary whole lines, not because any line was over budget.
  tet30 …/facts.jsonl — 21 lines, first line 882 B, over-budget line at position 15 (574898 B). A plain read releases 2 whole lines, 11976 B.
  tet29 …/facts.jsonl — 11 lines, first line 1273 B, over-budget line at position 2 (57249 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1273 B.
  tet28 …/facts.jsonl — 10 lines, first line 1237 B, over-budget line at position 2 (34477 B). A plain read releases 1 whole line, 1237 B.

So on all four, a plain `look <path>` returns between 1237 and 24947 bytes of whole lines and the floor does not fire. The floor fires when and only when the FIRST line of the selection is itself over budget, which on these four is reachable from exactly five ranges: `--lines 11:B` and `--lines 15:B` on tet46, `--lines 15:B` on tet30, `--lines 2:B` on tet29 and `--lines 2:B` on tet28 (any B at or past that line). A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.",
1445:   "text": "Working tree pin for this design: branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof, HEAD c821b94d6e1fbf4dc43a1691c975e440448534d2 ("check: report prose that moved while the claims it cites stood still"), `git status --porcelain -b` shows only the branch line, i.e. no modified, staged or untracked files.",
1456:   "text": "`prose_after_proof` (src/checks.rs, doc comment through the function body) computes, per non-heading prose block with a non-empty current citation list: `first_proof[claim]` = the EARLIEST evidence record whose `proposition_digest` exactly equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition and whose verdict is not `Refutes` (an empty/pre-digest digest does not qualify; `Qualifies` does); `anchor` = the MAX of `first_proof` over those cited claims that have one, with an existential gate `if cited.is_empty() { continue }` skipping the block entirely when no cited claim is in proof; `block_timestamp` = the timestamp of the EARLIEST event in the block's history whose text AND cite-list BOTH equal the current ones (`min_by_key` over `filter(|(_,t,c,_)| t == cur_text && c == cur_cite)`), with that event's own `why` carried alongside. The block is listed iff `block_timestamp > anchor`. Because `first_proof` is a per-claim minimum, the anchor can only rise when a cited claim that previously had NO first proof acquires one; a later record grading a claim already in proof does not move it.",
1467:   "text": "Where a new workspace event can live, tested three ways.

(1) SCHEMA: `ProseEvent` in src/prose.rs carries `#[serde(tag = "event")]` with exactly two variants, `Create` and `Revise`. Both variants' later-added fields (`before` on Create, `cite` on Revise) use `#[serde(default)]` with comments stating "an old log replays exactly as it did" — i.e. field-level forward compatibility is established practice within a variant.

(2) READER: `workspace::read_jsonl` in src/workspace.rs treats a missing file as empty and skips blank lines, but maps ANY line's `serde_json::from_str` failure to `Err(io::Error::InvalidData)` and returns it — the whole log fails, no line is skipped.

(3) EXPERIMENT: I created a scratch workspace `tet61lab` whose prose.jsonl held one valid `{"event":"Create",...}` line followed by one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, then ran the build at this pin (`cargo run --bin tetel -- query prose --workspace tet61lab`). Output: `tetel: error querying: unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise` at line 1 column 14`, exit 1. So a build that does not know a new tag value cannot read the log AT ALL — including the pre-existing Create line. The scratch workspace was then deleted (`rm -rf`, confirmed absent) and `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.

(4) SNAPSHOT MANIFEST: `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES` in src/snapshot.rs is a `const [&str; 9]` explicitly enumerating the shipped files (facts/claims/prose/targets/transplants .jsonl, counters.json, pending.json, refusals.log, identity.json), with a doc comment saying it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`." The same module's doc comment states "Because `render` is deterministic in the workspace alone, a snapshot either re-renders its memo byte-for-byte or it does not", and commits the project to "a rendered memo is never hand-edited."",
1559:   "text": "Two things that constrain how an ack's claim-digest component may be computed.

(1) src/checks.rs lines 336-368, `prose_after_proof`'s doc comment section "Two inputs, and the one that fails silently if swapped": `claims` "must be the ones `check_file` already imports from the *rendered document* (`ledger::import`), **never** the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`. Every `proposition_digest` on record was computed over a ledger-derived proposition, and the two are not the same string: rendering a claim into the ledger table (`compose::ledger_cell`) replaces embedded newlines with spaces, and importing (`ledger::split_row_cells`) trims every cell. Handed `claims.jsonl`'s propositions instead, a claim whose text has an embedded newline or edge whitespace would digest to something no record ever matches, this function would call it never in proof, and every block citing it would silently drop out of the list — with nothing red anywhere to say so." The same doc comment's "Existential, not universal" section records that requiring every citation to be in proof "was tried first and rejected".

(2) src/lib.rs lines 160-195, the call site. `findings.mint_windows = facts::mint_windows(&snapshot_dir);` sits immediately above, then the prose call, whose comment states `ledger.claims` is "deliberately used here, not the snapshot's `claims.jsonl`". The comment then defends reading prose.jsonl under `if let Ok(...)`: that silent skip is acceptable ONLY because "This is the same file `snapshot::check` already read moments ago, at the top of this function, via the identical `workspace::read_jsonl::<ProseEvent>` call inside `compose::render` -> `prose::load_all` (same path, same target type). A `prose.jsonl` that fails to parse here therefore already failed that earlier read too, and `findings.provenance` is already `Unreadable`, which `machine_check_failed` already reddens under `[provenance-drift]` — loudly, before this block runs. This `Err` arm is reachable only alongside a failure already reported elsewhere, never on its own". A test `check_a_corrupted_prose_jsonl_reddens_via_provenance_drift_not_silently` in tests/authoring_cli.rs is named as pinning that.",
1658:   "text": "`compose::render` (src/compose.rs lines 79-96) builds the memo from exactly five workspace logs: `prose::load_all`, `claims::load_all`, `targets::load_all`, `transplants::load_all` and `facts::load_all`. It reads nothing else. Since provenance drift is decided by re-rendering the snapshot and comparing bytes, only those five of the nine shipped snapshot files are drift-covered; `counters.json`, `pending.json`, `refusals.log` and `identity.json` are shipped but never re-rendered, so tampering with them is not drift. `identity.json` is one of these, and it is the file that decides whether the report calls a claim self-grounded or independently grounded. So a shipped-but-not-drift-covered snapshot file that changes what the report says is a category that already exists at this pin, with four members.",

4281:     "Rule 3 is not implementable as the comparison this claim decides on. Ran the worktree's own binary as `brief --json` over every memo in docs/design: 87 claims across five ledgers (tet28/29/30/46/47), and ZERO carry a `pin` \u2014 `render_json` emits the field only when `Claim::pin` is `Some`, so `find_stated_pin` returns None for every document in this corpus, TET-47's own included. Meanwhile every witnessed record in tet30's ledger carries `Some(\"sha256:...\")`. The comparison therefore has no second operand anywhere it would run: either None short-circuits and rule 3 is dead code that never fires on any existing memo, or Some != None and every claim of every existing memo is permanently owed under rule 3 alone \u2014 which discharges the entire cost saving the design is for. The claim's own qualifier \"answerable on ledgers already written\" is the part that fails: the ledgers are written, the memos have no stated pin to answer against. The design states neither behaviour for the None case."
4285:     "Second, independent refutation of the same clause: the two values compared are not the same kind of thing. src/facts.rs lines 405-452 constructs a fact's pin as `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending entry's label, world_root, world_state and output \u2014 a content fingerprint of the observation, with no relation to any commit id. src/ledger.rs lines 150-205 takes the claim's pin as the last backticked token after the word \"pin\" in the prose window before the ledger table, under the documented corpus convention \"at pin `71c0fd1`\" \u2014 a git short hash typed by an author. So even on a memo that did state a pin, the comparison is `sha256:<64 hex>` against `71c0fd1`, which is unequal by construction. The claim's premise \u2014 that the stored pin is \"the tree it stood in\" \u2014 treats a content hash of one fact's captured bytes as a tree identifier; two facts taken in the same checkout at the same commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ, which is nearly always."
4289:     "The load-bearing identification is wrong on two counts. (1) A witnessed record's `pin` is `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending extent entry's label + world_root + world_state + output (src/facts.rs:414-436) \u2014 a content fingerprint of the observation, not \"the tree it stood in\". The tree it stood in is carried by a different field, `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, and it is that field, not `pin`, that carries the doc comment the proposition quotes (\"Nothing reads it yet. It is written now so the question it exists for \u2014 *was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?* \u2014 becomes measurable at all\"). (2) A claim's currently stated pin is the backticked token parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` \u2014 a short git hash such as `abc1234`/`deadbee` in the crate's own tests. A `sha256:`-prefixed observation fingerprint can never equal one, so \"a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written\" would fire on every witnessed-grounded claim unconditionally rather than detecting a re-pin. The comparison the design wants is against `world`. Two subsidiary clauses do hold: no check reads the record pin today (F5), and folding the pin into `sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` would indeed drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof` (F3). \"Every evidence record already stores a pin\" is also too strong on the ingested path, where `RecordInput.pin` is `#[serde(default)] Option<String>` and a record written without one stores `None`."

4685:   "prop": "Because one parsed pin is assigned to every claim under a ledger table, a pin change is a document-level event: rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it, so it is a re-pin detector for the memo rather than a per-claim scheduling condition.",
4689:     "The premise is exactly right \u2014 `import` parses one `Option<String>` per ledger table and clones it into every `Claim` under that table, so the *stated* pin side of the comparison is uniform across the table. The conclusion drawn from it, \"rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it\", does not follow, because rule 3 compares the stated pin against a value stored per *record*, and records accumulate per claim. Immediately after a re-pin the disjunction holds; once any subset of claims has been re-graded against the new pin, their records carry it and the rule fires on the remainder only \u2014 i.e. it becomes precisely the per-claim scheduling condition the proposition says it is not. The weaker reading (\"a pin change is a document-level event\") is supported; the strict all-or-none clause is not."
4693:     "The inference is invalid as given; the conclusion survives only degenerately. \"One parsed pin is assigned to every claim\" establishes uniformity on ONE side of rule 3's comparison. Whether the comparison's result is uniform across the table depends on the other side too, and that side is not uniform: tet30's single ledger holds 61 distinct record pin values, and every one of its 13 claims carries records with several different pins (C11: 16 distinct). A record's pin is the grounder's own fact fingerprint (src/facts.rs 405-452), minted per observation, so it varies per record, per claim and per pass. \"Rule 3 fires for every claim in the table or for none of it\" is therefore true today only because the two operands are drawn from disjoint namespaces and never match at all \u2014 a vacuous uniformity, not the document-level re-pin detector the claim describes. Make the comparison meaningful in any way, and a claim last graded by a pass standing at the memo's pin and a claim last graded by a pass standing elsewhere get different answers within the same table, which is exactly the per-claim behaviour this claim rules out."

The evidence-blindness contract is stated in the code, but by build's own doc comment, not by the module doc's shape sentence."

6146:     "The census counts are right; the instruction to the implementer is not sized right, and this is the row that tells an implementer what to touch. The claim describes `brief_file`'s change as its \"whole signature today is a path and a bool\" plus a floor parameter threaded through two front ends. Read in lib.rs, `brief_file` also never calls `evidence::load`, never calls `analyze_ledger`, and never touches `snapshot::snapshot_path` or `workspace::identity_of` \u2014 every one of which the shipping predicate needs, since rules 1 and 2 are analyze_ledger outputs (C4), the floor counts digest-matched witnessed records (C24), and the undeterminable-attribution rule keys on the three-arm AuthoringIdentity (C10). Those four acquisitions are the substance of the change to `brief_file`, and none is a parameter. The census also does not reach them: `analyze_ledger`'s row is justified as \"single call site means a one-site change\", which is true of exposing its return value and false of the second call site this design adds; and `snapshot_path`/`identity_of`/`evidence::load` are not censused targets at all. An implementer sizing this row as written would build a signature change and discover a second ledger-analysis driver."

6733:     "Every number reproduces on an independent re-run (35/51/60/67 gradings, 0/5/6/7 discoveries), but the one the design leans hardest on carries no information. A \"discovery\" is defined in this replay as a cross-workspace regrade giving a verdict no EARLIER workspace gave, so its ordinal is at least 2 for any ledger that could ever be replayed; the observed ordinals are [2,2,2,2,2,3,4]. Capping at one workspace per wording therefore retains zero discoveries by identity, on this ledger and on every other, including one where a floor would be worthless. 6928:   "prop": "The owed predicate as decided here: a claim is owed iff it is in `analyze_ledger`'s `ungrounded_claims`, or in its `out_of_proof`, or the pin stored on its records differs from the memo's currently stated pin, or fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have a record whose `proposition_digest` equals the current proposition's, or `citation_ids_in` finds in its proposition text the id of a claim that is itself owed \u2014 the last computed to a fixpoint. Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot, and each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes.",
6932:     "The third disjunct of the decided predicate is not well defined, on two counts, and the claim's closing sentence (\"each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes\") does not hold for it. (a) \"The pin stored on its records\" is written as a single value; it is not. Replay of tet30's ledger: 125 records, 61 distinct pin values in that one file, and all 13 claims carry records with more than one distinct pin \u2014 C11 has 16, C10 and C12 have 8 each. The predicate does not say whether rule 3 fires when any, all, or the latest of a claim's record pins differs, and the three answers give different owed sets. (b) The comparison is between a per-fact `sha256:` content fingerprint (src/facts.rs 405-452) and a prose-parsed git token (src/ledger.rs 150-205), so no crate set is being reused here \u2014 unlike disjuncts 1, 2 and 4, this one is a new predicate over records, and it is the only disjunct with no existing computation behind it. Disjuncts 1, 2, 4 and 5 are unaffected by this record."
6936:     "Four of the five disjuncts hold as stated and the closing summary is right for them. The third disjunct is not: \"the pin stored on its records\" is, on the witnessed path, `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `sha256:` + a hash over each extent entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (src/facts.rs:414-436) \u2014 never a VCS revision, whereas \"the memo's currently stated pin\" is a git hash parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` (the crate's own tests assert `abc1234` and `deadbee`). Compared directly, the two can never be equal, so this disjunct fires unconditionally on every witnessed-grounded claim rather than detecting a re-pin; the field that actually records the tree an observation was taken against is `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, not `pin`. The final sentence is also over-broad on that disjunct: \"each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes\" is true of rule 1 (`ungrounded_claims`), rule 2 (`out_of_proof`) and rule 4 (`by_others` inside `grounding_provenance`), but not of rule 3 \u2014 no check in the crate reads a record's pin at all (F5), so there is no computed set to reuse. \"Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot\" is true as written (F7)."
6964:     "The two checkable structural clauses hold in analyze_ledger: the first two disjuncts are its own `ungrounded` and `out_of_proof` outputs, and the digest-matched set the third needs (`fresh`) is a local that is never returned, so exposing it rather than recomputing is exactly what keeps one definition of \"graded on this wording\". The load-bearing sense of \"witnessed\" is confirmed at the record layer separately \u2014 `pass` is the workspace identity on the captured path and caller-typed free text on the ingested one. The four-disjunct predicate itself is the design's decision, not a fact of the tree; nothing I read contradicts it, and the pin rule's exclusion is independently supported by the marker replay."

7647:     "True of the bound in isolation; false of the design, and the prose spends the unqualified form. `facts::mint` computes the pin as sha256 over, for every pending entry, `label` + `world_root` + `world_state` + `output` (facts.rs:417-435, its own comment: \"a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker\"), and copies `label` into the fact's extent (facts.rs:400-411). C17 requires the `Search` label to gain a \"showed N of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound)\" segment, and C20 requires the same of the `look_path` label. So for any observation on which the bound bites, the extent bytes change, the pin changes, and the snapshot's facts.jsonl changes \u2014 the exact three things this claim says stay byte-identical to today's, and on which the memo rests \"what makes f3 cheap and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope\". F2 shows the crate already reasons this way: the test comment at authoring_cli.rs:508-510 justifies naming memos in the label precisely so that two differently-excluded searches \"would not pin identically\".\n\nThe second half is the implementer-facing bite. This claim's mechanism is that `printed` and the pending entries \"are built separately... neither reads the other\" \u2014 today true, and F1(5) confirms the `Search` label is computed from `root`, `pattern`, `by_file.len()` and `note`, none of which touch `printed`. After the change the label must carry N, a number that exists only as a product of bounding `printed`. The design therefore creates the coupling this claim says is absent, and an implementer who took the claim at face value (\"a bound imposed while assembling `printed` cannot reach the buffer\") would bound `printed` and leave the label alone \u2014 which is the design's own defect back again.\n\nWhat survives unqualified: the captured `output`, the key and the world markers do stay byte-identical, so overlap and re-resolvability are untouched (F1(2),(3): `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads kind/pattern/key/world_root and never the label, and `scope::extent_covers` only enlarges its haystack)."

8648:   "prop": "The bound earns its own `NON_COVERAGE` line rather than being folded into an existing one. The list already discriminates a withholding tetel chose (the tetel-output exclusion) from platform accidents that \"contemplate nothing tetel chose\" (grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files); a bound tetel applies to its own return is of the first kind. What the line states is a gap `check` genuinely cannot close: a fact's extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it \u2014 `scope.rs` names that limit as permanently out of reach and does not claim otherwise.",
8668:     "The claim's own generalising argument does not stop where the claim stops it, and the standing line it specifies will mislead by contrast.\n\nC15 argues correctly that a `NON_COVERAGE` line phrased about a search \"would leave every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in the list, which is the one surface this design nominates for the general case\", and concludes the line must say: \"what `look` returned to its author is bounded, and a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it.\"\n\nRun that argument one step further. `look` is not the only verb that writes an observation into the pending buffer and hands its author a return the caller then cuts. `run` does the same: `run_command` captures the child's merged stdout/stderr, pushes a `Proc` PendingEntry whose `output` is that capture, and returns it whole and unmeasured; both front ends hand it straight back with no size check \u2014 `print!(\"{}\", outcome.printed)` at src/main.rs:526 and `\"output\": outcome.printed` at src/mcp.rs:653-656 (F3). The `run` tool's own description at src/mcp.rs:649 documents the large case explicitly (\"a command whose output is enormous \u2026 puts that in a repository forever\"). So a `run` observation has precisely the defect this design exists to remove \u2014 the coupling between what was captured and what the author saw is broken by the caller, silently \u2014 and after f3 it is not merely unfixed but affirmatively contrasted against, because the new standing line names `look`.\n\nThe condition C15 does not state: its second half \u2014 \"a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it\" \u2014 is true of every fact in the ledger regardless of which verb captured it, but the line as specified scopes it to `look`. A reader of `check`'s standing non-coverage will reasonably infer the caveat does not apply to `run`-captured facts, which is exactly backwards: those are the ones with no bound, no shortfall segment and no trace at all.\n\nNot a demand that f3 bound `run` \u2014 that is a scoping decision the design may keep. What is owed is either a line whose general half is not verb-scoped, or a stated reason why `run` is excluded from a statement the design itself calls the general case."
8672:     "The verifiable parts hold. The standing list does discriminate a chosen withholding from platform accidents, and its comment says verbatim \"A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here\", beside the entry naming grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files. The first half's factual load is correct: `run_command` returns the child's whole captured output unmeasured with no length test anywhere in the function, and both front ends hand it back whole (`print!(\"{}\", outcome.printed)` in main.rs's Run arm; `\"output\": outcome.printed` in the MCP run tool); the run tool's own description does contemplate \"a command whose output is enormous\" and answers by warning rather than bounding. `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering at all.\n\nThe qualification is the clause \"`scope.rs` names that second half as permanently out of reach\". The only occurrence of \"permanently out of reach\" in the whole of src/ is src/scope.rs:42, and what it registers there is a different proposition: \"Whether the note is *correct* about the location it names is exactly the limit this project registered as permanently out of reach (\\\"insincere examination\\\" \u2014 capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation).\" That is about the truth of an author's interpretation of a location, not about how much of a capture the author was shown. Reading it as naming the second half (\"a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it\") requires stretching \"insincere examination\" from not-examined to not-shown, and scope.rs does not spell that out. This matters because it is the clause carrying the memo's assurance that the new entry \"names an old limit that had been invisible rather than admitting a new weakness\" \u2014 after the bound, `look` genuinely shows the author less than the extent records, which is new. Separate, non-blocking: the list itself is `NON_COVERAGE` in src/report.rs:86, not in scope.rs; C15 does not misattribute it, but the two files are easy to conflate here."

Reconciling over that constant leaves a tenth file a newer build wrote entirely unvisited by an older build's render, so the snapshot means \"the workspace at last render, for the files the rendering build's manifest names, plus whatever any other build left behind\" \u2014 which is the equality the claim says the fix establishes, and it is not established for the file this design adds. Reconciling over the snapshot directory instead does establish it, at the price of an older build deleting snapshot content it does not understand \u2014 a cost this memo never weighs, and a direct tension with `SNAPSHOT_FILES`' stated purpose that shipping or withholding a file be a deliberate per-build decision. Note the same residual hazard is what C14 cites to kill the withdrawal verb, so the two claims are consistent only under the manifest reading \u2014 under which this sentence's stated purpose is not achieved."

10248:     "Every asymmetry this claim names is in the source as written. mcp.rs:355 declares `text: String` with neither Option nor #[serde(default)] (every sibling optional field carries the attribute), so a missing text fails deserialisation before the handler's open_workspace/dispatch \u2014 no workspace::refuse is reached; main.rs's Command::Prose declares `text: Option<String>`, so the CLI does not. Both CLI text-consuming arms (Revise, Paragraph) call resolve_text_or_stdin(..., text.as_deref()), whose None case reads stdin, so a flagless ack would block \u2014 hence the positioning requirement. --level is indeed a separate CLI flag consumed only by the heading arm while ProseParams folds selector and value into one heading_level, so an enumeration written against the MCP shape would miss it; excluding --why, the other mode-bearing flags are exactly the six named. Both front ends select mode with an if/else-if chain building one variant and dropping fields it lacks (main.rs:782-809, mcp.rs:738-744), and prose.rs's own revise doc records the earlier instance of that defect (--cites \"accepted alongside --revise and silently discarded\"). Of the ack's refusals, exactly two pre-exist in prose::revise: the nonexistent-block refusal and `why.trim().is_empty()` backing \"--revise requires --why (revisions must explain themselves)\"; creation is ungated per the module doc, so heading/citation/claim-resolution gates are new."

10392:   "prop": "An acknowledgement must not enter `render`'s output. Keeping the rendered bytes a function of facts, claims, prose, targets and transplants only \u2014 with `acks.jsonl` shipped by the snapshot copy loop but never read by `compose::render` \u2014 preserves the determinism the provenance-drift finding rests on, and buys a property that makes the required re-render honest rather than merely tolerable: re-rendering after an ack and nothing else rewrites the snapshot in place, since existing snapshot files are overwritten, while leaving the memo byte-identical. The discharge therefore shows up in version control as a change to the record and no change to the argument, which is exactly what it is.",
10400:     "`compose::render` reads exactly prose, claims, targets, transplants and facts and nothing else, so keeping `acks.jsonl` out of it leaves the rendered bytes unchanged; and `snapshot::write`'s doc states \"Existing files are overwritten: re-rendering a memo replaces its snapshot\" (F2), so a re-render after an ack rewrites the snapshot in place while producing a byte-identical memo."

2704:   "prop": "\"Transcribed verbatim\" cannot be an honour-system field, and does not need to be: the decidable relation is that a premise's text is refused unless it is a verbatim substring of the cited donor fact's captured output. Both sides of that comparison are Strings the tool controls \u2014 a fact's output is produced only by look/run (file bytes read verbatim by look_path, grep match lines, a process's merged stream), no authoring surface lets anyone supply output by hand, and output is immutable after mint \u2014 so substring containment is a pure byte-level comparison with no normalisation step owned by the check. Typing is the selection mechanism, not the trust: the author types the premise, but a typed premise the donor never wrote fails containment and is refused at the verb. 2926:   "prop": "The strictness objections to byte-level containment dissolve on the actual capture path, and every weaker relation reopens the invention channel. A donor comment wrapped across lines with interior prefix noise (`//`, `*`, indentation) IS a contiguous byte substring of a look_path capture, because look_path stores the file's bytes verbatim \u2014 the cost is only that the selected premise carries its comment syntax into the rendered section, which the \"never paraphrase\" constraint endorses rather than tolerates. Stripping that noise would require knowing each language's comment syntax, which is precisely the hard-coded per-language coupling scope.rs's \"language-agnostic by construction\" doctrine excludes. Two capture modes genuinely fight containment \u2014 grep-derived match outputs interleave \"lineno:\" prefixes between lines, and whole-search/no-match records carry empty output \u2014 so the design's guidance is that a donor fact is minted from `look` of the donor file; that is guidance about which observation to select from, not a new rule, since the relation is indifferent to which kind produced the bytes. Weaker relations fail: per-line containment lets an author stitch non-adjacent lines into a sentence the donor never wrote, and whitespace- or case-normalised matching means the memo shows text the capture does not contain \u2014 both are paraphrase with extra steps.",

3112:   "prop": "Containment against a fact's whole output has one genuine unsoundness, and it is fixable by the same schema move TET-28 already made. Fact.output is built at mint by joining the buffer entries' non-empty outputs with \"\\n\", and the per-entry boundaries are not stored \u2014 so \"substring of fact.output\" can be satisfied by text straddling the seam between two observations: bytes that were never contiguous in anything the author actually saw, e.g. the tail of one file's capture concatenated with the head of another's. The fix is a serde-defaulted per-entry field on ExtentEntry recording the entry's output byte length, mirroring exactly how kind and pattern were added for TET-28: boundaries become reconstructible from lengths (skipping zero-length entries, matching the mint-time filter), the premise relation is then \"verbatim substring of a single observation's output\", and a donor fact minted before the field existed is ineligible with the same remedy TET-28 gives legacy facts \u2014 re-look and re-mint. Absent means not recorded, never guessed.",

3612:   "prop": "The refusals land on three surfaces, each the earliest that can decide its own question. (1) At the verb: quotation invariants \u2014 donor fact exists and is span-eligible, premise text is a verbatim substring of a single observation's output, destination is a live target, a discharge names an existing live claim. These are per-record and decidable at creation, exactly like target's census refusal. (2) At `render --out`: completeness \u2014 a live transplant with an undischarged premise (none cited, or its discharge claim withdrawn) refuses the write. This is deliberately later than the verb (the intermediate state is legal while authoring) and deliberately earlier than check (the ticket's placement): --out is the act that writes the reviewable artifact and its snapshot under the pinned policy that a rendered memo is never hand-edited, so a memo with a declared-but-unexamined premise should fail to come into existence rather than exist and fail; the remedy is singular \u2014 discharge the premise, or withdraw it or its transplant with --why. A preview render (no --out) still assembles, marking undischarged rows loudly, so mid-work visibility is preserved; this render/--out asymmetry is new, and it is the design's most debatable departure. (3) At check: re-verification of everything above against the shipped snapshot \u2014 both directions, since tampering can go either way (a transplant row the snapshot lacks; a snapshot premise whose text is not contained in its donor fact's output; a premise whose discharge claim is withdrawn or missing) \u2014 as a machine failure in the same partition as uncensused targets, with rows in a snapshotless document reported human-owed as unverifiable, the standing choice for snapshot-dependent findings. Containment is re-checked byte-for-byte from facts.jsonl, which already ships full outputs; check runs nothing and fetches nothing to do it.",

5804:   "prop": "There is no digest-shaped alternative in the sharp sense, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded, whereas nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block \u2014 not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput` \u2014 and the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it is supposed to grade blind. A weaker, genuinely clock-free alternative is constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record \u2014 per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it \u2014 so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. A publication log samples state only at the renders the author happens to perform, so a prose edit and the grading that preceded it inside one publication interval are indistinguishable, and the FORK-94 shape \u2014 grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render \u2014 falls entirely inside a single interval and would be missed. 10624:   "prop": "Every evidence record already stores a pin \u2014 on the witnessed path the pin of the grounder's own fact, i.e. the tree it stood in, written expressly so that \"was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?\" becomes measurable \u2014 in a field no check reads today; so rule 3 is implementable as a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written, whereas folding the pin into `sha256_hex` would change every pinned claim's current digest and drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof`.",
10628:     "Rule 3 is not implementable as the comparison this claim decides on. Ran the worktree's own binary as `brief --json` over every memo in docs/design: 87 claims across five ledgers (tet28/29/30/46/47), and ZERO carry a `pin` \u2014 `render_json` emits the field only when `Claim::pin` is `Some`, so `find_stated_pin` returns None for every document in this corpus, TET-47's own included. Meanwhile every witnessed record in tet30's ledger carries `Some(\"sha256:...\")`. The comparison therefore has no second operand anywhere it would run: either None short-circuits and rule 3 is dead code that never fires on any existing memo, or Some != None and every claim of every existing memo is permanently owed under rule 3 alone \u2014 which discharges the entire cost saving the design is for. The claim's own qualifier \"answerable on ledgers already written\" is the part that fails: the ledgers are written, the memos have no stated pin to answer against. The design states neither behaviour for the None case."
10632:     "Second, independent refutation of the same clause: the two values compared are not the same kind of thing. src/facts.rs lines 405-452 constructs a fact's pin as `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending entry's label, world_root, world_state and output \u2014 a content fingerprint of the observation, with no relation to any commit id. src/ledger.rs lines 150-205 takes the claim's pin as the last backticked token after the word \"pin\" in the prose window before the ledger table, under the documented corpus convention \"at pin `71c0fd1`\" \u2014 a git short hash typed by an author. So even on a memo that did state a pin, the comparison is `sha256:<64 hex>` against `71c0fd1`, which is unequal by construction. The claim's premise \u2014 that the stored pin is \"the tree it stood in\" \u2014 treats a content hash of one fact's captured bytes as a tree identifier; two facts taken in the same checkout at the same commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ, which is nearly always."
10636:     "The load-bearing identification is wrong on two counts. (1) A witnessed record's `pin` is `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending extent entry's label + world_root + world_state + output (src/facts.rs:414-436) \u2014 a content fingerprint of the observation, not \"the tree it stood in\". The tree it stood in is carried by a different field, `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, and it is that field, not `pin`, that carries the doc comment the proposition quotes (\"Nothing reads it yet. It is written now so the question it exists for \u2014 *was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?* \u2014 becomes measurable at all\"). (2) A claim's currently stated pin is the backticked token parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` \u2014 a short git hash such as `abc1234`/`deadbee` in the crate's own tests. A `sha256:`-prefixed observation fingerprint can never equal one, so \"a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written\" would fire on every witnessed-grounded claim unconditionally rather than detecting a re-pin. The comparison the design wants is against `world`. Two subsidiary clauses do hold: no check reads the record pin today (F5), and folding the pin into `sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` would indeed drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof` (F3). \"Every evidence record already stores a pin\" is also too strong on the ingested path, where `RecordInput.pin` is `#[serde(default)] Option<String>` and a record written without one stores `None`."
10640:     "Everything structural holds \u2014 a fact's pin is `sha256:` over each observation entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (a content fingerprint, not a tree identifier); a claim's pin is a backticked prose token; every witnessed record's predicate carries the deduped world markers of the fact's extent; `check` reads the authoring tree states out of the shipped facts.jsonl; and `world` is present on `Predicate` but absent from `EvidenceRecord`, so it is dropped at read-back in `parse_line`. The clause that fails is the count. Replaying `brief --json` over the five rendered memos at this commit gives 15 + 14 + 13 + 19 + 27 = 88 claims, not 87, with zero `pin` keys among them. The \"missing from all\" property is exact; the population is 88."

On the absent second operand I confirmed the four memos other than the one under grading carry no `pin` in `brief --json` (0 of 61 items), and the grounding brief for the fifth prints no `pin:` line for any of its 32 claims, so the corpus figure holds for all five."
10660:     "Both halves check out as written. The fact pin is `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each entry's label, world_root, world_state and output \u2014 a content fingerprint. And `brief --json` over all five rendered memos yields 89 claims with zero `pin` keys, so the claim-side operand is universally absent; the disjunction the proposition draws from that (never fires, or every claim permanently owed) follows."
10668:     "The measured half is right and the conclusion survives, but the universal the claim reaches for is false. \"The comparison has no second operand anywhere it would run\" is asserted from a survey of the five tetel-RENDERED memos. It does not hold on the other population the tool serves: `brief --json` over tests/fixtures/ledger_check.md, an imported hand-authored ledger, returns both claims carrying \"pin\": \"abc1234\", and tests/brief_cli.rs:53 asserts that the document-level pin is attached to each claim. On an imported ledger the operand is present, so the rule would run rather than short-circuit, and the two-case split the claim closes on (\"either the absent value short-circuits and the rule never fires, or it reads as a mismatch and every claim of every existing memo is permanently owed\") is missing that case. Rule 3 should still be dropped \u2014 a git short-hash lifted from prose and a sha256 content fingerprint over an observation's labels and output are different kinds of value and would mismatch wherever the comparison did run \u2014 but the ground is kind-mismatch, not universal absence, and this matters more now that the other stated ground for dropping rule 3 (C29's \"unsatisfiable forever after\") does not hold."
10672:     "Holds only for WITNESSED records, a restriction the proposition does not state. C6 asserts flatly that \"a record's pin is a fact's `sha256:` fingerprint\" and that the two pins \"can never be equal, so on the imported population the comparison fires on every claim always\". `record` has two write paths and only the witnessed one sets `pin: Some(fact.pin.clone())`. On the ingested path `build_statement` sets `pin: input.pin.clone()` from `RecordInput.pin`, caller-supplied free text copied verbatim with no shape check (F1). The imported population is precisely where claim pins exist \u2014 the crate's own fixture pins both claims `abc1234` \u2014 so a reporter filing an ingested record there may type `abc1234` and the two pins are equal. On that population the comparison therefore does not fire always; it is dischargeable by naming, which is the same defect C24 names for `pass` and which it fixes by counting witnessed records only. Rule 3's section never applies that restriction. The decision to drop rule 3 survives, but the reason as written is wrong for half the population it invokes: the correct statement is that the comparison is either vacuous (tetel-rendered, no claim pin) or discharge-by-typing (imported, ingested records), not that it always fires."
10676:     "`brief --json` on tests/fixtures/ledger_check.md returned exactly two claims, both `\"pin\": \"abc1234\"` \u2014 a git-short-hash-shaped token typed into prose \u2014 while a witnessed record's pin is `Some(fact.pin.clone())` and a fact's pin is `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each entry's label, world_root, world_state and output. The two forms can never be byte-equal, so a kind-mismatch comparison fires on every pinned claim always."
10680:     "Second population confirmed: across the four other rendered memos' 61 briefed claims not one item carries a `pin` key, so on the tetel-rendered population the comparison fires on none."
10684:     "Witnessed pin is Some(fact.pin), and a fact's pin is \"sha256:\" + sha256 over each extent entry's label, world_root, world_state and output; ledger_check.md's two claims both take the prose pin abc1234; build_statement copies input.pin verbatim with no validation."
10688:     "Witnessed record pin = fact pin = \"sha256:\" + hash over labels/world markers/output; claim pin = a backticked token parsed from prose, `abc1234` on both claims of the ledger_check.md fixture; the two shapes cannot be equal. build_statement copies input.pin with no shape check, so the unrestricted reading is discharge-by-typing."
10705:   "prop": "Every evidence record already stores a pin \u2014 on the witnessed path the pin of the grounder's own fact, i.e. the tree it stood in, written expressly so that \"was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?\" becomes measurable \u2014 in a field no check reads today; so rule 3 is implementable as a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written, whereas folding the pin into `sha256_hex` would change every pinned claim's current digest and drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof`.",
10709:     "Rule 3 is not implementable as the comparison this claim decides on. Ran the worktree's own binary as `brief --json` over every memo in docs/design: 87 claims across five ledgers (tet28/29/30/46/47), and ZERO carry a `pin` \u2014 `render_json` emits the field only when `Claim::pin` is `Some`, so `find_stated_pin` returns None for every document in this corpus, TET-47's own included. Meanwhile every witnessed record in tet30's ledger carries `Some(\"sha256:...\")`. The comparison therefore has no second operand anywhere it would run: either None short-circuits and rule 3 is dead code that never fires on any existing memo, or Some != None and every claim of every existing memo is permanently owed under rule 3 alone \u2014 which discharges the entire cost saving the design is for. The claim's own qualifier \"answerable on ledgers already written\" is the part that fails: the ledgers are written, the memos have no stated pin to answer against. The design states neither behaviour for the None case."
10713:     "Second, independent refutation of the same clause: the two values compared are not the same kind of thing. src/facts.rs lines 405-452 constructs a fact's pin as `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending entry's label, world_root, world_state and output \u2014 a content fingerprint of the observation, with no relation to any commit id. src/ledger.rs lines 150-205 takes the claim's pin as the last backticked token after the word \"pin\" in the prose window before the ledger table, under the documented corpus convention \"at pin `71c0fd1`\" \u2014 a git short hash typed by an author. So even on a memo that did state a pin, the comparison is `sha256:<64 hex>` against `71c0fd1`, which is unequal by construction. The claim's premise \u2014 that the stored pin is \"the tree it stood in\" \u2014 treats a content hash of one fact's captured bytes as a tree identifier; two facts taken in the same checkout at the same commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ, which is nearly always."
10717:     "The load-bearing identification is wrong on two counts. (1) A witnessed record's `pin` is `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `format!(\"sha256:{}\", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending extent entry's label + world_root + world_state + output (src/facts.rs:414-436) \u2014 a content fingerprint of the observation, not \"the tree it stood in\". The tree it stood in is carried by a different field, `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, and it is that field, not `pin`, that carries the doc comment the proposition quotes (\"Nothing reads it yet. It is written now so the question it exists for \u2014 *was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?* \u2014 becomes measurable at all\"). (2) A claim's currently stated pin is the backticked token parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` \u2014 a short git hash such as `abc1234`/`deadbee` in the crate's own tests. A `sha256:`-prefixed observation fingerprint can never equal one, so \"a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written\" would fire on every witnessed-grounded claim unconditionally rather than detecting a re-pin. The comparison the design wants is against `world`. Two subsidiary clauses do hold: no check reads the record pin today (F5), and folding the pin into `sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` would indeed drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof` (F3). \"Every evidence record already stores a pin\" is also too strong on the ingested path, where `RecordInput.pin` is `#[serde(default)] Option<String>` and a record written without one stores `None`."
10721:     "Everything structural holds \u2014 a fact's pin is `sha256:` over each observation entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (a content fingerprint, not a tree identifier); a claim's pin is a backticked prose token; every witnessed record's predicate carries the deduped world markers of the fact's extent; `check` reads the authoring tree states out of the shipped facts.jsonl; and `world` is present on `Predicate` but absent from `EvidenceRecord`, so it is dropped at read-back in `parse_line`. The clause that fails is the count. Replaying `brief --json` over the five rendered memos at this commit gives 15 + 14 + 13 + 19 + 27 = 88 claims, not 87, with zero `pin` keys among them. The \"missing from all\" property is exact; the population is 88."

11039:   "prop": "Because one parsed pin is assigned to every claim under a ledger table, a pin change is a document-level event: rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it, so it is a re-pin detector for the memo rather than a per-claim scheduling condition.",
11043:     "The premise is exactly right \u2014 `import` parses one `Option<String>` per ledger table and clones it into every `Claim` under that table, so the *stated* pin side of the comparison is uniform across the table. The conclusion drawn from it, \"rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it\", does not follow, because rule 3 compares the stated pin against a value stored per *record*, and records accumulate per claim. Immediately after a re-pin the disjunction holds; once any subset of claims has been re-graded against the new pin, their records carry it and the rule fires on the remainder only \u2014 i.e. it becomes precisely the per-claim scheduling condition the proposition says it is not. The weaker reading (\"a pin change is a document-level event\") is supported; the strict all-or-none clause is not."
11047:     "The inference is invalid as given; the conclusion survives only degenerately. \"One parsed pin is assigned to every claim\" establishes uniformity on ONE side of rule 3's comparison. Whether the comparison's result is uniform across the table depends on the other side too, and that side is not uniform: tet30's single ledger holds 61 distinct record pin values, and every one of its 13 claims carries records with several different pins (C11: 16 distinct). A record's pin is the grounder's own fact fingerprint (src/facts.rs 405-452), minted per observation, so it varies per record, per claim and per pass. \"Rule 3 fires for every claim in the table or for none of it\" is therefore true today only because the two operands are drawn from disjoint namespaces and never match at all \u2014 a vacuous uniformity, not the document-level re-pin detector the claim describes. Make the comparison meaningful in any way, and a claim last graded by a pass standing at the memo's pin and a claim last graded by a pass standing elsewhere get different answers within the same table, which is exactly the per-claim behaviour this claim rules out."

13635:     "Every number reproduces on an independent re-run (35/51/60/67 gradings, 0/5/6/7 discoveries), but the one the design leans hardest on carries no information. A \"discovery\" is defined in this replay as a cross-workspace regrade giving a verdict no EARLIER workspace gave, so its ordinal is at least 2 for any ledger that could ever be replayed; the observed ordinals are [2,2,2,2,2,3,4]. Capping at one workspace per wording therefore retains zero discoveries by identity, on this ledger and on every other, including one where a floor would be worthless. So \"a rule with no confirmation floor would have retained none of the seven\" does not measure the floor's necessity \u2014 it restates the definition. Likewise N=4 retaining all seven is fixed by the maximum observed ordinal being 4. The empirical content of the replay is the ordinal distribution and the cost curve, and that content supports the weaker and still-useful proposition the memo could have made: five of the seven arrive at the second workspace, so N=2 buys 5/7 for 16 extra gradings. The sentence \"the floor is therefore what carries the discovery property\" is the one that spends the definitional figure as though it were an observation. Context worth stating: only 16 of the 35 pairs were ever graded by two or more distinct workspaces at all."
13643:     "Every figure reproduces on an independent replay of tet30's ledger: 35 (claim, digest) pairs, 69 unbounded workspace-gradings, 7 discoveries at ordinals 5/1/1, the curve 35/51/60/67 at N=1..4, and N=2 buying five of the seven for sixteen gradings above the dirty-only floor. The final clause does not hold. \"Each further N buys less\" is false at the step this design's default turns on: N=2->N=3 costs 9 gradings for 1 discovery, N=3->N=4 costs 7 gradings for the last 1. The marginal price per discovery falls from nine to seven, so returns are not monotonically diminishing in cost, and the run also shows N=4 retaining all seven discoveries at 67 of the 69 gradings full re-grading performs \u2014 a cap at 4 forgoes nothing and saves two. The prose at memo line 11, \"every further step buys less for more\", carries the same error. This matters because that monotonicity is the stated reason for stopping low; the measured curve supports a floor over no floor, and supports 2 over 1, but does not support 2 over 3 or 4 by diminishing returns."
