Deletion loses a distinction the crate elsewhere insists on keeping: a report from which an acknowledged block has vanished cannot be told from a report on a memo where no post-proof revision ever happened, and this is a tool whose no-rows path exists precisely to say that two states which happen to both be quiet are not the same state. The cost of printing is also already paid \u2014 the entry format carries an author's own reason verbatim today, under `revised because:`, with the source comment insisting it is never paraphrased and calling it the most actionable line the entry has.",
1472:   "text": "Underneath those is the property that makes the rest cheap to reason about: the acknowledgement is a filter applied to the trigger's output, never an input to it. The set of blocks a reader is asked to act on can only shrink, so the design cannot invent a demand. A stale ack and an unmatched ack both simply fail to suppress, which is indistinguishable from no ack at all. A corrupt one is the case I first waved through and should not have. The line reader turns any bad line into an error over the entire log, and the one place this crate swallows that silently \u2014 the prose log at check time \u2014 defends the silence with a premise that does not transfer: that a corrupt prose log has already reddened provenance before the check gets there. Keeping acks out of `render` is precisely what makes that false for this file. So an unreadable acknowledgement log has to redden, joining the existing rule that drift and an unreadable snapshot are machine failures because both are objective contradictions decidable without a human. That is the single point where this design touches the machine partition, and it touches it for corruption of the record rather than for anything an acknowledgement means. It is also worth being clear what the digests do not buy: keying on them does not close TET-30's conceded blind spot for prose that ships alongside a claim revision. It only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.",
1521:   "text": "Because the residue is computed against a snapshot and the snapshot is written by `render --out`, an ack minted after a render is invisible until the next one. That sequencing is not new and it is not this design's to fix: everything the check sees about a workspace it sees through the snapshot. What is this design's to decide is whether the acknowledgement changes the memo's bytes, and it must not \u2014 the determinism of `render` in the workspace alone is what makes a drift finding mean anything. Keeping acks out of the rendered output turns the extra render from an annoyance into a useful signal: it rewrites the snapshot in place and leaves the document byte-identical, so the discharge lands in version control as a change to the record with no change to the argument. That is a true description of what an acknowledgement is.",

103:   "text": "So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the ticket hoped for exists. Two were examined; both fail, and no claim is made that a third could not be found. The sharp one \u2014 a record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for, the exact analogue of `out_of_proof` \u2014 cannot be built, for a structural reason rather than an oversight. `out_of_proof` compares digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded. No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape, and the brief a pass receives is id, proposition and pin. Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind, which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line. The weaker one is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away: `render --out` could append a publication record \u2014 each prose block's text digest, each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it \u2014 and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all. It is rejected on resolution, and the reason is structural too. A log that samples only when the author renders cannot order two events that fall inside one interval, and a grading followed by a prose edit followed by a single render is one interval. On the ticket's own account, that is the shape the finding took. The clock-free formulation would have been silent on it. That is the trade, stated plainly: the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering an interval-sampled log cannot, and pays for it with a bound it prints.",
129:   "text": "The last open question asks whether this is a line or a section, and the answer is neither exactly: it is bullets in the flat human-owed list, one per listed block, with a single preamble bullet ahead of them. There are no sub-headings in that partition today, so a section would be the only one and would announce by its shape that it outranks everything beside it. The preamble carries the one thing constant across the entries \u2014 that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same \u2014 and it is printed once rather than per bullet for the reason this crate already recorded when it collapsed `no scope declared` to a single document-level line: repeating a constant per row buries the findings that are actually about the document. Each entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because a block's id is never written into the rendered output and an id alone points at something the reader cannot find; that mapping comes from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render`, so the block-to-line correspondence is described once. The entry then names each cited claim with its first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp \u2014 the inputs to the comparison, printed so a reader can disagree with the conclusion rather than having to trust it.",
168:   "text": "One measurement made in passing deserves recording, because the next ticket in this family will meet it. Declaring these six targets required six whole-worktree searches, and a census captures its entire output into a fact that ships in the snapshot. This repository's previous two snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines \u2014 tet29's longest is 57249 bytes, tet28's 34477 \u2014 so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps. What such a search costs turns out to be a property of the instrument and the moment rather than of the symbol, in two separate ways. Scope: `render` matches 486 lines and 373271 bytes of this tree in the state the census was taken in, or 447 and 311672 with `.git/` and `target/` excluded as well; `NON_COVERAGE` 35 and 95637, `Findings` 23 and 57418, `check_file` 5 and 285, and the two symbols that do not exist yet nothing at all. Those numbers hold still because the trees they range over are frozen. Time: the same counts taken with this memo's own artifacts included do not hold still at all. `render` measured 529 lines and 1136689 bytes at one point in this memo's review and 550 and 1202134 later, with no source change in between \u2014 what grew was this memo's evidence log, now 59 records and 164392 bytes, and its snapshot, whose longest fact line is the 574898-byte capture of the `render` census itself. Grading a claim about census cost enlarges the thing the claim is about, which is the compounding thesis demonstrating itself. It is also the one part of this section no independent pass can confirm, along with the count of six searches: both range over this memo's own logs and snapshot, which a pass grading this memo must not open, so they are recorded here expecting to stay ungraded. What any pass can check, and what survives every way of scoping the count, is the ordering and its cause: censusing a symbol quoted at length in prior memos' captured snapshots costs orders of magnitude more than censusing one that appears only in source. `check_file` is this crate's own entry point, dispatched from both front ends, and returns 5 lines and 285 bytes \u2014 so what drives the cost is not whether the crate talks about a symbol but whether earlier memos captured text quoting it, and every memo added under `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of anything those memos quote.",
224:   "text": "This memo was written against a single tree: commit b57bf8edb4c1eb59d8d86a8327179f43a9cb0829, \"design: anchor the residue at first proof, not at the last pass\", with no tracked source file differing from it. The reader who wants to re-take an observation should check that pin out first. Which tree each individual observation was actually taken against is not something this memo asserts \u2014 every observation carries its own working-tree marker, and `check` prints those states.",
276:   "text": "The disclosure goes in the whole-search record's label, and it costs nothing in schema. TET-28 already added exactly one record per `look --grep` whose job is to say where a search started rather than what it hit \u2014 a `Search` entry when the grep matched, a `NoMatch` entry when it did not, and never both. That record is the natural and the only correct home for a statement about what the search did not visit, because the exclusion is a property of the search and not of any file it found. Putting the text there buys two carriers already built: the memo's Facts table renders each extent entry's label and renders nothing else from it, so the exclusion set is on the page for a reader who has only the committed document; and the pin hashes the label, so two searches with different exclusion sets fingerprint differently even when the text they matched is identical. It should also be printed in what `look` returns, for the author reading it in the moment \u2014 but the printed string is the convenience and the label is the record, which is the opposite of the two shapes this project has already been burned by: a warning with no lifecycle, and a refusal trail missing the refusal that mattered.",
289:   "text": "The ticket's numbers are figures reported inside a memo, which makes them claims that were graded rather than measurements anyone here has made, so the effect was re-measured on this tree directly. A census of the symbol `NON_COVERAGE` over the tetel worktree returns 858,096 bytes from fifteen files. Fourteen of those files are tetel's own output \u2014 three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot logs \u2014 and one, `src/report.rs`, is the source anybody grepping for that symbol wanted. With the three exclusions the same census returns 169 bytes from `src/report.rs` alone. Those are bytes grep handed back and bytes a fact would then store; what fraction of them reaches any given caller is a separate quantity, and a later section settles it, because the ticket's answer to it does not survive.",
315:   "text": "This design ran into its own subject before it could declare a single modification target, and the shape of that is worth stating rather than working around quietly. TET-28 requires a symbol an implementer is told to modify to be censused by a grep of the whole worktree. Every candidate symbol here was priced first: `look_grep` costs 709,469 bytes, `NON_COVERAGE` 858,096, `censuses` 691,562, `look_path` 688,776, `search_key` 633,291. The interesting number is not any one of them but the floor they share \u2014 roughly 0.63 MB is returned whichever symbol is asked for, because it is not about the symbol at all. Dropping snapshot directories and evidence ledgers alone removes between 95.9% and 99.9% of each. So the census requirement is today priced by tetel's own accumulated output rather than by the code being censused: two thirds of a megabyte comes back from grep, and is stored in the fact, per declared target.",
328:   "text": "Then the design paid the price once, deliberately, to declare `look_grep` \u2014 and the payment failed in a way that settles the ticket's sharpest question. The search ran and was recorded, but the harness returning results to the author refused to hand back 707,751 characters across 38 lines, and spilled them to a file. So this memo's author never read the output of their own census, while the fact minted anyway and the full 707,751 characters are shipping in the snapshot beside this document. The ticket asked any design to say which path it is changing, the return path or the retention path, and this is the answer from the inside: they are already separable, only the return path currently has a cap, that cap belongs to the harness rather than to tetel, and it fired. The census's own extent is the summary of the problem \u2014 ten files matched, eight of them tetel's own output, two of them the source anyone grepping for `look_grep` was looking for.",
445:   "text": "The ticket's sharpest question is whether the non-stationarity actually goes away, and the answer is no \u2014 it moves, and moving it is the point. Rendering a second memo into a scratch tree, touching no source, left the matched output of a search for the same symbol byte-identical while changing the exclusion list from one memo pattern to two. So the half the ticket complained about within a run is genuinely gone: an evidence ledger growing during grading cannot perturb a census any more, because the search never reaches it. But the exclusion set itself is a function of how many memos the tree holds, the design writes that set into the search record's label, and the label is inside the pin \u2014 so two censuses of one symbol against unchanged source will still pin differently either side of a render. That is not a leak that survived; it is the same fact about the world, moved out of the captured bytes where nobody could see it and into a sentence in the record where a reader comparing two pins is told immediately why they differ.",
458:   "text": "Nothing, and the answer has two halves, both of which can be shown rather than argued. The first is that the change cannot reach the check path at all: two exhaustive greps of the whole source tree find `Command::new` in only `observe.rs` \u2014 the grep inside `look_grep`, and `run_command`'s child \u2014 and `worldstate.rs`, where it runs git; and `observe::` in only `main.rs` and `mcp.rs`, which build a request and dispatch it, and `facts.rs`, where the single occurrence sits in a doc comment. Every other file in `src/` contains neither string, so nothing on the check or render path calls into the observe module or spawns a process. The second half is that there would be nothing to change even if it could: the `tetel fact` module states that extent, output and pin are set once at mint time and never appear in a revision event at all, so no code path exists that could rewrite them. The three committed memos keep the extents and pins they were minted with, whatever a `look` would do today.",
497:   "text": "This design was built against a pinned worktree, so every file range and command output cited below can be re-opened at that commit and read as this memo read it. One commit landed mid-run \u2014 the memo's own first rendering \u2014 and a few later observations were taken after it; it touched nothing under `src/` or `tests/`, so the source tree the memo reasons about is the same at both.",
562:   "text": "The ticket asks whether the fix for the pin defect is to digest the pin or to compare it separately. Neither, and the reason splits by which record wrote the pin. On the witnessed path \u2014 the only one the floor counts \u2014 a record's pin is a content fingerprint over an observation's labels, world markers and output, while a claim's pin where it exists is a git short hash lifted from prose; the crate's own fixture ledger is where the operand does exist, both its claims pinned `abc1234`. Those two can never be equal, so the comparison fires on every claim always where a claim pin exists, and on none of the memos this tool renders, where no claim carries one. On the ingested path it is worse rather than better: the pin is copied straight from caller-supplied input with no shape check, so a reporter could type `abc1234` and discharge the comparison by typing \u2014 the same defect the floor sidesteps by counting witnessed records only. Under either reading the comparison carries no information about whether a wording has been graded.",
575:   "text": "The channel itself is not what the ticket supposed. Asked to confirm that a claim's pin moves only when its citation list moves, the code says otherwise: nothing derives a claim's pin from the facts it cites. The pin is read out of the prose \u2014 a sentence of the form \"at pin `<hash>`\" sitting between the nearest heading and the ledger table \u2014 and the single value found there is stamped onto every claim in that table. That parser is for imported, hand-authored ledgers; it finds nothing in a memo this tool rendered, which is the first half of why rule 3 needed rebuilding.",
618:   "text": "Dropping the rule does not mean dropping the defect the ticket found. The divergence is real and it has a home: carry the predicate's world markers into `EvidenceRecord` \u2014 one field at read-back, in a type named on twenty-two lines across two modules \u2014 and let `check` report which tree each grading pass stood in beside the tree the memo's own facts were taken against. One branch must not be collapsed on the way: the ingested write path sets the marker list to empty unconditionally, with no input that could do otherwise, so an empty set means the tree is unknown and not that it differs. That is the same empty-as-value trap the visibility line has on its identity axis, and it wants the same treatment. Reported this way the observation is a fact a reader weighs, not a unit of work a pass completes by grading, which is exactly what the human-owed partition is for. It took this section three tries to reach a ground that survives, and the two it discarded were both claims of impossibility that this repository's own artifacts disprove.",
683:   "text": "Neither matcher covers both populations, but that is a fact about the two tried here and not an obstacle in the problem \u2014 a rule matching a hyphenated id while still finding the corpus's bare references is straightforward to write. What decides the question is yield, and the yield is not merely small but uncountable. One figure holds: no proposition in any rendered memo carries a bracketed citation-shaped id. Bare tokens naming a sibling id resist even being totalled. The count moves with tokenisation; it moves with reading, according to whether an endpoint of \"per C3-C5\" counts, whether a backticked `ungrounded: C99` counts, and whether \"tet28's C9\" is a sibling reference or a mention of another memo's claim; and it moves with ordinary editing, as this memo showed by rewording one of its own claims mid-run and dissolving a reference in passing. This design applied a standard to rule 3 \u2014 a rule that fires on nothing ever written here is not worth shipping \u2014 and it would be dishonest not to turn the same standard on a disjunct carrying a new reverse index, a traversal and borrowed machinery to schedule a set nobody can count twice the same way. The closure is deferred, and what it owes before it returns is a stated yield, not a better matcher.",
696:   "text": "One thing is worth recording about the machinery the closure would have needed, since it was built and then set aside. Check 5 already indexes the reverse citation graph and walks it breadth-first with a visited set seeded by the root, precisely so a citation cycling back terminates instead of looping, and that traversal transfers to a fixpoint over owed-ness cleanly \u2014 its two stated preconditions, that a self-citation is not a dependency and that ledger claims are excluded, both turn out not to bind at that destination. None of that is wrong. It simply has nowhere to land while the closure is deferred, which is why this memo carries no transplant.",
709:   "text": "The ticket suspects that N=2 and a rule to stop after the first round that provokes no revision may together prevent a design loop from terminating on its intended signal, since the first round cannot leave nothing owed. Within this design there is no conflict to have: the owed list is an input to a pass's schedule, no disjunct of the predicate reads it back, and nothing this feature writes records whether it was ever emptied. An owed list still non-empty when a run stops is therefore work declined, not an exit criterion unmet. Whether it also composes with the stopping rules a designer agent operates under is a question about that agent's own definition file, which lies outside this repository and cannot be checked from it \u2014 so this memo names it rather than answering it.",
761:   "text": "The blast radius of that extension is small, and the way this memo first got it wrong is worth keeping. By identifier, `grounding_provenance` is named in three files: its definition, field and zero-init in `checks.rs`, one call site in `lib.rs`, one printing loop in `report.rs`. From that this design concluded no test depends on its wording, which is false. Grep the strings the function emits rather than its name and two end-to-end test files appear, asserting on `SELF-GROUNDED` and on `cannot be determined from here`, one of them asserting the latter's absence. They are substring assertions and an appended count would probably survive them, but that is luck, not the census's doing. A census enumerates a symbol's occurrences and is silent about everything that depends on what the symbol produces \u2014 its own declared blind spot, and this memo walked into it.",
839:   "text": "Replaying the scheduling rule against that ledger is what shows the floor is load-bearing, but one figure has to be set aside first. That a floor of one retains none of the seven findings is true by construction: a discovery is a verdict no earlier workspace gave, so it cannot occur at the first workspace to read a wording, on this ledger or on any other. The measurement that means something is what happens above one. Seven substantive verdict changes occurred at all; five of them arrived from the second workspace, one from the third, one from the fourth; and capping distinct workspaces per wording costs 35, 51, 60 and 67 gradings at N of one to four, against 69 unbounded. So N=2 buys five of the seven for sixteen gradings, and every further step buys less for more. The floor is not a safeguard bolted onto a cost optimisation \u2014 it is the part of the rule that decides how much of what full re-grading was buying survives.",
865:   "text": "The ticket asks for four pieces to ship together, and it is worth being exact about the standing of each. One is measured: the replay's ordinal distribution and cost curve say what a floor of two buys and at what price. That is not the same as the figure the earlier draft of this memo led with \u2014 that a floor of one finds nothing \u2014 which follows from how a discovery is defined rather than from anything this ledger did. The closure and the visibility line are argued in this memo from what the code does, and nothing measures what their absence would cost. The fourth, pin-change detection, does not ship as a scheduling rule at all. Extending the measurement's standing to what is only argued would be the easiest way for this design to sound better than it is, so it does not.",
891:   "text": "That divergence is worth naming rather than smoothing over. On the correctness axis it is survivable for a reason specific to what an owed list is: the schedule settles nothing, no value of N marks a claim confirmed, and the full brief goes out unchanged whatever N is. On the discovery axis it is not benign, because the amount of grading scheduled is what decides how many findings a run would still reach. Two obligations follow. The floor in force must be printed by both renderers \u2014 cheap in text, not cheap in JSON, where the brief is a bare top-level array with nowhere for a document-level value to sit, so carrying it means wrapping the array in an object and breaking the contract the `--json` test asserts. This design takes that breakage deliberately rather than let the floor be invisible under one output mode. The second obligation is a stated default: both front ends reach the brief today with no floor argument at all, so a caller who supplies nothing must receive a defined value. That value is 2, chosen for the largest saving rather than because it is the only floor that saves \u2014 18 gradings of 69 against 9 at N=3, giving up two of the seven discoveries where N=3 gives up one. Whether that last one is worth nine gradings is a judgement the replay does not make, and a memo whose stakes answer it differently raises N. That is the whole reason the floor is a parameter.",
904:   "text": "The earlier drafts of this section stopped here and reported the question as undecided, on the grounds that a memo under active work has a reproducible marker while one whose repository had moved on never would again. The second half of that was simply wrong: a marker belongs to a commit, and a commit stays reachable. With the false half removed the question is decided rather than open, which is why this section now ends in a decision instead of a stopping rule.",
930:   "text": "One asymmetry the design cannot close, and should not hide. Every figure in the replay counts gradings not performed, and a grading is not performed only if some pass declines to perform it. Nothing here makes that happen. A brief emits an id, a proposition, an optional pin and a withheld scope per claim, with no instruction prose in either renderer, and the invariant that keeps every claim in the list is the same one this design refused to touch. The owed section is therefore an artifact a pass may act on, not a mechanism that reduces what it grades. The costs on the other side are unconditional, and the largest of them was missing from an earlier draft: `brief_file` today reads a memo and renders it, calling neither `evidence::load` nor `analyze_ledger` and touching neither the snapshot path nor the workspace identity, so giving it the owed list turns it into a second ledger-analysis driver \u2014 a change of kind, not a threaded parameter. Add the floor through two front ends, a shape change to the JSON brief, and the widenings in the check path. The saving is real only if passes use the list, and no claim here says they will, because nothing in this repository could check it.",
969:   "text": "This memo designs one change with two halves. `look` decides for itself how much of an observation it returns to the author, and it says what it withheld in two places: in the observation's label, where a later reader of the memo finds it, and in the returned text itself, where the author finds it before writing anything about what they saw. The worktree everything below was read against is pinned: HEAD 81137aa683bdced9bf01a94d34c66b7f4a1758fd on branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof, with every tracked path unmodified and unstaged and the only entries `git status` reports at all being the eleven untracked files this design itself wrote \u2014 the memo, its evidence sidecar and its snapshot directory. So a reader can re-run any of it against the same tracked bytes. Which of those states each individual fact was captured in is not asserted here: tetel records it with the fact and `check` reports it.",
982:   "text": "`look_grep` already does the two jobs separately. It runs grep once, then builds `printed` \u2014 the string handed back to the author, which today is grep's stdout verbatim followed by a parenthesised exclusion note \u2014 and, independently, the pending entries: one `Search` record carrying the root, the pattern and a matched-file count, and one `GrepMatch` record per matched file carrying that file's matched lines. The two are derived from the same stdout but neither reads the other, and that separation is what the bound rests on: out of a bounded call, every entry's captured output, its key and its world-tree markers come back byte-identical to what they are today, so two observations of one root still overlap and a later reader still re-reads the same bytes. What does not stay identical is the extent, the pin and the fact that ships. `facts::mint` copies each entry's label straight into the extent and hashes label, world markers and output into the pin, and this design writes a shortfall segment into the label \u2014 so wherever the bound bites, all three differ from what they would otherwise have been. That is the point and not a cost. It is the same property the exclusion note was given when TET-46 chose to list the skipped memo paths rather than count them, so that two searches withholding different things could not fingerprint alike; a bounded search and a whole one should not fingerprint alike either. What makes f3 cheap, and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope, is narrower than \"nothing changes\": no new record, no second pass over the buffer, nothing read back out of the entries, no signature touched. One number is computed while `printed` is being assembled, and the label is built from that number. The direction matters to whoever implements this \u2014 bound first, label from the bound. An implementer who bounds `printed` and leaves the label alone has rebuilt the silent cut this memo exists to remove.",
1047:   "text": "The other `look` path turns out to have a different answer from the one its shape suggests. `look_path` computes `shown` and uses it twice, but not as one value in one place: `printed` is a string of its own that receives a *copy* of `shown` by borrow, and only afterwards is `shown` moved into the pending entry's `output`. Two independent strings exist between those two points, so a bound applied to `printed` there leaves the captured output, the label, the key, the extent, the pin and the snapshot byte-identical \u2014 the same separation `look_grep` has, in a function that reads at first glance as though it has none. There is therefore no code-shaped reason to leave the plain `look <path>` alone, and no other reason either: a whole-file read that overruns the caller's cap is the same silent cut this design exists to stop. So it is bounded too, on the same terms.",
1099:   "text": "Carrying that mechanism across brings its two preconditions with it. The donor states that a shortfall is not an error, and the same must hold here: hitting the bound returns a successful outcome with a bounded body, not a refusal. The code does not force that, and it is worth being exact about why, because the ordering invites the opposite reading: `printed` is assembled before any pending entry exists and the buffer is saved as the last act before the return, so an implementation that bounded while building `printed` could refuse there and discard nothing. What settles it is the crate's own rule about when to refuse. A refusal is for the case where nothing is left to tell and the remedy is singular \u2014 that is exactly how TET-28's census refusal justifies itself, against a check that stayed human-owed because only a person could tell context from conclusion \u2014 and every refusal in this crate's source is of that kind, a missing input or a forbidden flag combination, never a measurement of a result. A byte budget is not that: the number is a judgement, and an author who trips it has no act that re-runs the census smaller. Refusing would take the census away and name nothing to do instead. The donor also states that its key is the resolved path regardless of the range requested, which is what keeps two differently-sized reads of one file overlapping. That holds at the destination too: the `Search` entry is keyed by its root and each match entry by its file, both from paths alone, so a bounded search and an unbounded one of the same root overlap exactly as two unbounded ones would.",
1159:     "why": "For every valid explicit range, the code formats a range annotation; clamping is only applied when the requested end exceeds the file length.",
1169:      "why": "The code shows that whenever --lines is provided with valid bounds, it formats a range annotation '{path} lines {a}-{end}' regardless of whether clamping occurred. The line 'let end = b.min(total);' performs the clamping operation, but the format statement that follows executes for all valid ranges, not just clamped ones. If the author's stated convention were implemented, requesting lines 1-100 from a 200-line file would produce no range annotation, but the code would produce '{path} lines 1-100'."
1262:   "text": "All source observations below were taken against one worktree state: branch `tet30-prose-revised-since-proof` at commit `c821b94`, the commit that shipped TET-30's `prose-revised-since-proof` residue. The pin record at the head of this memo's evidence captured `git status` printing nothing at all. No tracked file was modified afterwards; nothing here was implemented. The tree has since gained exactly three paths, all of them this work's own output and all untracked: the memo, its snapshot, and its evidence ledger.",
1305:   "text": "The sketch left the event's home open between `prose.jsonl` and a sibling log. The evidence closes it, and not on grounds of taste. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged enum over two variants, and the workspace's line reader turns any single unparseable line into an error over the entire log. A third variant is therefore not a compatible addition: I wrote a scratch workspace whose prose log held one ordinary `Create` followed by one `Ack`, and the build at this pin refused the whole file \u2014 including the `Create` it understood perfectly well. Every older build encountering such a snapshot would lose its ability to read prose at all, which is a far worse outcome than the residue line this design exists to clear. The field-level `#[serde(default)]` precedent already in both variants does not extend to a new variant.",
1318:   "text": "So the event lives in its own append-only log, `acks.jsonl`, and the snapshot manifest gains a tenth entry. Three properties, between them, make the failure direction one-way, and the third is the one I had to be shown twice. The manifest is the first: it is an explicit enumeration precisely so that shipping a new workspace file is a decision rather than an accident, so a build predating the entry never opens the file and prints exactly the listing TET-30 shipped. The second is that the ack log only grows, which holds cheaply here because the file does not exist yet: nothing in the tool today can remove or truncate a file it has never heard of, its only writer will be an appending verb, and no withdrawal verb ships. That was where an earlier draft of this section stopped, and stopping there was wrong. Monotonicity is a property of one workspace's log; the mechanism runs over a snapshot. Nothing binds a memo to the workspace that rendered it \u2014 the flag is free on every invocation \u2014 and the writer skips a file the current workspace lacks rather than removing it. So render a memo once from a workspace holding an acknowledgement, then again from a workspace that never held one \u2014 a rebuilt state directory, a second machine \u2014 and the old ack log survives beside the new prose and claims. That is a superset, not a prefix, and it suppresses a block the true state would list, silently. The third property closes it: the ack records the identity of the workspace that minted it, and suppression requires that identity to match the one the snapshot ships. A log from elsewhere is then void rather than honoured, and the failure returns to over-reporting.",
1359:   "text": "The brief called deletion and annotation both doctrine-compatible, and they are not equally good. Deletion loses a distinction the crate elsewhere insists on keeping: a report from which an acknowledged block has vanished cannot be told from a report on a memo where no post-proof revision ever happened, and this is a tool whose no-rows path exists precisely to say that two states which happen to both be quiet are not the same state. The cost of printing is also already paid \u2014 the entry format carries an author's own reason verbatim today, under `revised because:`, with the source comment insisting it is never paraphrased and calling it the most actionable line the entry has.",
1424:   "text": "Underneath those is the property that makes the rest cheap to reason about: the acknowledgement is a filter applied to the trigger's output, never an input to it. The set of blocks a reader is asked to act on can only shrink, so the design cannot invent a demand. A stale ack and an unmatched ack both simply fail to suppress, which is indistinguishable from no ack at all. A corrupt one is the case I first waved through and should not have. The line reader turns any bad line into an error over the entire log, and the one place this crate swallows that silently \u2014 the prose log at check time \u2014 defends the silence with a premise that does not transfer: that a corrupt prose log has already reddened provenance before the check gets there. Keeping acks out of `render` is precisely what makes that false for this file. So an unreadable acknowledgement log has to redden, joining the existing rule that drift and an unreadable snapshot are machine failures because both are objective contradictions decidable without a human. That is the single point where this design touches the machine partition, and it touches it for corruption of the record rather than for anything an acknowledgement means. It is also worth being clear what the digests do not buy: keying on them does not close TET-30's conceded blind spot for prose that ships alongside a claim revision. It only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.",
1463:   "text": "Because the residue is computed against a snapshot and the snapshot is written by `render --out`, an ack minted after a render is invisible until the next one. That sequencing is not new and it is not this design's to fix: everything the check sees about a workspace it sees through the snapshot. What is this design's to decide is whether the acknowledgement changes the memo's bytes, and it must not \u2014 the determinism of `render` in the workspace alone is what makes a drift finding mean anything. Keeping acks out of the rendered output turns the extra render from an annoyance into a useful signal: it rewrites the snapshot in place and leaves the document byte-identical, so the discharge lands in version control as a change to the record with no change to the argument. That is a true description of what an acknowledgement is.",

88:   "text": "So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the ticket hoped for exists. Two were examined; both fail, and no claim is made that a third could not be found. The sharp one \u2014 a record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for, the exact analogue of `out_of_proof` \u2014 cannot be built, for a structural reason rather than an oversight. `out_of_proof` compares digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded. No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape, and the brief a pass receives is id, proposition and pin. Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind, which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line. The weaker one is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away: `render --out` could append a publication record \u2014 each prose block's text digest, each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it \u2014 and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all. It is rejected on resolution, and the reason is structural too. A log that samples only when the author renders cannot order two events that fall inside one interval, and a grading followed by a prose edit followed by a single render is one interval. On the ticket's own account, that is the shape the finding took. The clock-free formulation would have been silent on it. That is the trade, stated plainly: the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering an interval-sampled log cannot, and pays for it with a bound it prints.",
114:   "text": "The last open question asks whether this is a line or a section, and the answer is neither exactly: it is bullets in the flat human-owed list, one per listed block, with a single preamble bullet ahead of them. There are no sub-headings in that partition today, so a section would be the only one and would announce by its shape that it outranks everything beside it. The preamble carries the one thing constant across the entries \u2014 that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same \u2014 and it is printed once rather than per bullet for the reason this crate already recorded when it collapsed `no scope declared` to a single document-level line: repeating a constant per row buries the findings that are actually about the document. Each entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because a block's id is never written into the rendered output and an id alone points at something the reader cannot find; that mapping comes from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render`, so the block-to-line correspondence is described once. The entry then names each cited claim with its first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp \u2014 the inputs to the comparison, printed so a reader can disagree with the conclusion rather than having to trust it.",
153:   "text": "One measurement made in passing deserves recording, because the next ticket in this family will meet it. Declaring these six targets required six whole-worktree searches, and a census captures its entire output into a fact that ships in the snapshot. This repository's previous two snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines \u2014 tet29's longest is 57249 bytes, tet28's 34477 \u2014 so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps. What such a search costs turns out to be a property of the instrument and the moment rather than of the symbol, in two separate ways. Scope: `render` matches 486 lines and 373271 bytes of this tree in the state the census was taken in, or 447 and 311672 with `.git/` and `target/` excluded as well; `NON_COVERAGE` 35 and 95637, `Findings` 23 and 57418, `check_file` 5 and 285, and the two symbols that do not exist yet nothing at all. Those numbers hold still because the trees they range over are frozen. Time: the same counts taken with this memo's own artifacts included do not hold still at all. `render` measured 529 lines and 1136689 bytes at one point in this memo's review and 550 and 1202134 later, with no source change in between \u2014 what grew was this memo's evidence log, now 59 records and 164392 bytes, and its snapshot, whose longest fact line is the 574898-byte capture of the `render` census itself. Grading a claim about census cost enlarges the thing the claim is about, which is the compounding thesis demonstrating itself. It is also the one part of this section no independent pass can confirm, along with the count of six searches: both range over this memo's own logs and snapshot, which a pass grading this memo must not open, so they are recorded here expecting to stay ungraded. What any pass can check, and what survives every way of scoping the count, is the ordering and its cause: censusing a symbol quoted at length in prior memos' captured snapshots costs orders of magnitude more than censusing one that appears only in source. `check_file` is this crate's own entry point, dispatched from both front ends, and returns 5 lines and 285 bytes \u2014 so what drives the cost is not whether the crate talks about a symbol but whether earlier memos captured text quoting it, and every memo added under `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of anything those memos quote.",
192:   "text": "This memo was written against a single tree: commit b57bf8edb4c1eb59d8d86a8327179f43a9cb0829, \"design: anchor the residue at first proof, not at the last pass\", with no tracked source file differing from it. The reader who wants to re-take an observation should check that pin out first. Which tree each individual observation was actually taken against is not something this memo asserts \u2014 every observation carries its own working-tree marker, and `check` prints those states.",
244:   "text": "The disclosure goes in the whole-search record's label, and it costs nothing in schema. TET-28 already added exactly one record per `look --grep` whose job is to say where a search started rather than what it hit \u2014 a `Search` entry when the grep matched, a `NoMatch` entry when it did not, and never both. That record is the natural and the only correct home for a statement about what the search did not visit, because the exclusion is a property of the search and not of any file it found. Putting the text there buys two carriers already built: the memo's Facts table renders each extent entry's label and renders nothing else from it, so the exclusion set is on the page for a reader who has only the committed document; and the pin hashes the label, so two searches with different exclusion sets fingerprint differently even when the text they matched is identical. It should also be printed in what `look` returns, for the author reading it in the moment \u2014 but the printed string is the convenience and the label is the record, which is the opposite of the two shapes this project has already been burned by: a warning with no lifecycle, and a refusal trail missing the refusal that mattered.",
257:   "text": "The ticket's numbers are figures reported inside a memo, which makes them claims that were graded rather than measurements anyone here has made, so the effect was re-measured on this tree directly. A census of the symbol `NON_COVERAGE` over the tetel worktree returns 858,096 bytes from fifteen files. Fourteen of those files are tetel's own output \u2014 three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot logs \u2014 and one, `src/report.rs`, is the source anybody grepping for that symbol wanted. With the three exclusions the same census returns 169 bytes from `src/report.rs` alone. Those are bytes grep handed back and bytes a fact would then store; what fraction of them reaches any given caller is a separate quantity, and a later section settles it, because the ticket's answer to it does not survive.",
283:   "text": "This design ran into its own subject before it could declare a single modification target, and the shape of that is worth stating rather than working around quietly. TET-28 requires a symbol an implementer is told to modify to be censused by a grep of the whole worktree. Every candidate symbol here was priced first: `look_grep` costs 709,469 bytes, `NON_COVERAGE` 858,096, `censuses` 691,562, `look_path` 688,776, `search_key` 633,291. The interesting number is not any one of them but the floor they share \u2014 roughly 0.63 MB is returned whichever symbol is asked for, because it is not about the symbol at all. Dropping snapshot directories and evidence ledgers alone removes between 95.9% and 99.9% of each. So the census requirement is today priced by tetel's own accumulated output rather than by the code being censused: two thirds of a megabyte comes back from grep, and is stored in the fact, per declared target.",
296:   "text": "Then the design paid the price once, deliberately, to declare `look_grep` \u2014 and the payment failed in a way that settles the ticket's sharpest question. The search ran and was recorded, but the harness returning results to the author refused to hand back 707,751 characters across 38 lines, and spilled them to a file. So this memo's author never read the output of their own census, while the fact minted anyway and the full 707,751 characters are shipping in the snapshot beside this document. The ticket asked any design to say which path it is changing, the return path or the retention path, and this is the answer from the inside: they are already separable, only the return path currently has a cap, that cap belongs to the harness rather than to tetel, and it fired. The census's own extent is the summary of the problem \u2014 ten files matched, eight of them tetel's own output, two of them the source anyone grepping for `look_grep` was looking for.",
413:   "text": "The ticket's sharpest question is whether the non-stationarity actually goes away, and the answer is no \u2014 it moves, and moving it is the point. Rendering a second memo into a scratch tree, touching no source, left the matched output of a search for the same symbol byte-identical while changing the exclusion list from one memo pattern to two. So the half the ticket complained about within a run is genuinely gone: an evidence ledger growing during grading cannot perturb a census any more, because the search never reaches it. But the exclusion set itself is a function of how many memos the tree holds, the design writes that set into the search record's label, and the label is inside the pin \u2014 so two censuses of one symbol against unchanged source will still pin differently either side of a render. That is not a leak that survived; it is the same fact about the world, moved out of the captured bytes where nobody could see it and into a sentence in the record where a reader comparing two pins is told immediately why they differ.",
426:   "text": "Nothing, and the answer has two halves, both of which can be shown rather than argued. The first is that the change cannot reach the check path at all: two exhaustive greps of the whole source tree find `Command::new` in only `observe.rs` \u2014 the grep inside `look_grep`, and `run_command`'s child \u2014 and `worldstate.rs`, where it runs git; and `observe::` in only `main.rs` and `mcp.rs`, which build a request and dispatch it, and `facts.rs`, where the single occurrence sits in a doc comment. Every other file in `src/` contains neither string, so nothing on the check or render path calls into the observe module or spawns a process. The second half is that there would be nothing to change even if it could: the `tetel fact` module states that extent, output and pin are set once at mint time and never appear in a revision event at all, so no code path exists that could rewrite them. The three committed memos keep the extents and pins they were minted with, whatever a `look` would do today.",
494:   "text": "This design was built against a pinned worktree, so every file range and command output cited below can be re-opened at that commit and read as this memo read it. One commit landed mid-run \u2014 the memo's own first rendering \u2014 and a few later observations were taken after it; it touched nothing under `src/` or `tests/`, so the source tree the memo reasons about is the same at both.",
559:   "text": "The ticket asks whether the fix for the pin defect is to digest the pin or to compare it separately. Neither, and the reason splits by which record wrote the pin. On the witnessed path \u2014 the only one the floor counts \u2014 a record's pin is a content fingerprint over an observation's labels, world markers and output, while a claim's pin where it exists is a git short hash lifted from prose; the crate's own fixture ledger is where the operand does exist, both its claims pinned `abc1234`. Those two can never be equal, so the comparison fires on every claim always where a claim pin exists, and on none of the memos this tool renders, where no claim carries one. On the ingested path it is worse rather than better: the pin is copied straight from caller-supplied input with no shape check, so a reporter could type `abc1234` and discharge the comparison by typing \u2014 the same defect the floor sidesteps by counting witnessed records only. Under either reading the comparison carries no information about whether a wording has been graded.",
563:     "clause": "the comparison fires on every claim always where a claim pin exists, and on none of the memos this tool renders, where no claim carries one.",
564:     "why": "The captured code marks the evidence record's pin as unused and explicitly says that no check reasons inspect it, so a pin comparison does not currently fire.",
569:     "rejected": "    #[allow(dead_code)] // carried for fidelity; no check reasons over its value directly \u2014 see derived_kind\n    pub pin: Option<String>,",
572:      "why": "The author's text states that a comparison involving a 'pin' value \"fires on every claim always where a claim pin exists\". However, the evidence in F4 shows the definition of the `EvidenceRecord` struct, which is used when checking claims. In this struct, the `pin` field is decorated with `#[allow(dead_code)]` and accompanied by a comment stating `// carried for fidelity; no check reasons over its value directly`. This directly contradicts the author's description of the program's behavior, as the field that would be needed for such a comparison is explicitly marked as unused by the checking logic."
587:   "text": "The channel itself is not what the ticket supposed. Asked to confirm that a claim's pin moves only when its citation list moves, the code says otherwise: nothing derives a claim's pin from the facts it cites. The pin is read out of the prose \u2014 a sentence of the form \"at pin `<hash>`\" sitting between the nearest heading and the ledger table \u2014 and the single value found there is stamped onto every claim in that table. That parser is for imported, hand-authored ledgers; it finds nothing in a memo this tool rendered, which is the first half of why rule 3 needed rebuilding.",
630:   "text": "Dropping the rule does not mean dropping the defect the ticket found. The divergence is real and it has a home: carry the predicate's world markers into `EvidenceRecord` \u2014 one field at read-back, in a type named on twenty-two lines across two modules \u2014 and let `check` report which tree each grading pass stood in beside the tree the memo's own facts were taken against. One branch must not be collapsed on the way: the ingested write path sets the marker list to empty unconditionally, with no input that could do otherwise, so an empty set means the tree is unknown and not that it differs. That is the same empty-as-value trap the visibility line has on its identity axis, and it wants the same treatment. Reported this way the observation is a fact a reader weighs, not a unit of work a pass completes by grading, which is exactly what the human-owed partition is for. It took this section three tries to reach a ground that survives, and the two it discarded were both claims of impossibility that this repository's own artifacts disprove.",
695:   "text": "Neither matcher covers both populations, but that is a fact about the two tried here and not an obstacle in the problem \u2014 a rule matching a hyphenated id while still finding the corpus's bare references is straightforward to write. What decides the question is yield, and the yield is not merely small but uncountable. One figure holds: no proposition in any rendered memo carries a bracketed citation-shaped id. Bare tokens naming a sibling id resist even being totalled. The count moves with tokenisation; it moves with reading, according to whether an endpoint of \"per C3-C5\" counts, whether a backticked `ungrounded: C99` counts, and whether \"tet28's C9\" is a sibling reference or a mention of another memo's claim; and it moves with ordinary editing, as this memo showed by rewording one of its own claims mid-run and dissolving a reference in passing. This design applied a standard to rule 3 \u2014 a rule that fires on nothing ever written here is not worth shipping \u2014 and it would be dishonest not to turn the same standard on a disjunct carrying a new reverse index, a traversal and borrowed machinery to schedule a set nobody can count twice the same way. The closure is deferred, and what it owes before it returns is a stated yield, not a better matcher.",
726:   "text": "One thing is worth recording about the machinery the closure would have needed, since it was built and then set aside. Check 5 already indexes the reverse citation graph and walks it breadth-first with a visited set seeded by the root, precisely so a citation cycling back terminates instead of looping, and that traversal transfers to a fixpoint over owed-ness cleanly \u2014 its two stated preconditions, that a self-citation is not a dependency and that ledger claims are excluded, both turn out not to bind at that destination. None of that is wrong. It simply has nowhere to land while the closure is deferred, which is why this memo carries no transplant.",
739:   "text": "The ticket suspects that N=2 and a rule to stop after the first round that provokes no revision may together prevent a design loop from terminating on its intended signal, since the first round cannot leave nothing owed. Within this design there is no conflict to have: the owed list is an input to a pass's schedule, no disjunct of the predicate reads it back, and nothing this feature writes records whether it was ever emptied. An owed list still non-empty when a run stops is therefore work declined, not an exit criterion unmet. Whether it also composes with the stopping rules a designer agent operates under is a question about that agent's own definition file, which lies outside this repository and cannot be checked from it \u2014 so this memo names it rather than answering it.",
791:   "text": "The blast radius of that extension is small, and the way this memo first got it wrong is worth keeping. By identifier, `grounding_provenance` is named in three files: its definition, field and zero-init in `checks.rs`, one call site in `lib.rs`, one printing loop in `report.rs`. From that this design concluded no test depends on its wording, which is false. Grep the strings the function emits rather than its name and two end-to-end test files appear, asserting on `SELF-GROUNDED` and on `cannot be determined from here`, one of them asserting the latter's absence. They are substring assertions and an appended count would probably survive them, but that is luck, not the census's doing. A census enumerates a symbol's occurrences and is silent about everything that depends on what the symbol produces \u2014 its own declared blind spot, and this memo walked into it.",
869:   "text": "Replaying the scheduling rule against that ledger is what shows the floor is load-bearing, but one figure has to be set aside first. That a floor of one retains none of the seven findings is true by construction: a discovery is a verdict no earlier workspace gave, so it cannot occur at the first workspace to read a wording, on this ledger or on any other. The measurement that means something is what happens above one. Seven substantive verdict changes occurred at all; five of them arrived from the second workspace, one from the third, one from the fourth; and capping distinct workspaces per wording costs 35, 51, 60 and 67 gradings at N of one to four, against 69 unbounded. So N=2 buys five of the seven for sixteen gradings, and every further step buys less for more. The floor is not a safeguard bolted onto a cost optimisation \u2014 it is the part of the rule that decides how much of what full re-grading was buying survives.",
895:   "text": "The ticket asks for four pieces to ship together, and it is worth being exact about the standing of each. One is measured: the replay's ordinal distribution and cost curve say what a floor of two buys and at what price. That is not the same as the figure the earlier draft of this memo led with \u2014 that a floor of one finds nothing \u2014 which follows from how a discovery is defined rather than from anything this ledger did. The closure and the visibility line are argued in this memo from what the code does, and nothing measures what their absence would cost. The fourth, pin-change detection, does not ship as a scheduling rule at all. Extending the measurement's standing to what is only argued would be the easiest way for this design to sound better than it is, so it does not.",
921:   "text": "That divergence is worth naming rather than smoothing over. On the correctness axis it is survivable for a reason specific to what an owed list is: the schedule settles nothing, no value of N marks a claim confirmed, and the full brief goes out unchanged whatever N is. On the discovery axis it is not benign, because the amount of grading scheduled is what decides how many findings a run would still reach. Two obligations follow. The floor in force must be printed by both renderers \u2014 cheap in text, not cheap in JSON, where the brief is a bare top-level array with nowhere for a document-level value to sit, so carrying it means wrapping the array in an object and breaking the contract the `--json` test asserts. This design takes that breakage deliberately rather than let the floor be invisible under one output mode. The second obligation is a stated default: both front ends reach the brief today with no floor argument at all, so a caller who supplies nothing must receive a defined value. That value is 2, chosen for the largest saving rather than because it is the only floor that saves \u2014 18 gradings of 69 against 9 at N=3, giving up two of the seven discoveries where N=3 gives up one. Whether that last one is worth nine gradings is a judgement the replay does not make, and a memo whose stakes answer it differently raises N. That is the whole reason the floor is a parameter.",
934:   "text": "The earlier drafts of this section stopped here and reported the question as undecided, on the grounds that a memo under active work has a reproducible marker while one whose repository had moved on never would again. The second half of that was simply wrong: a marker belongs to a commit, and a commit stays reachable. With the false half removed the question is decided rather than open, which is why this section now ends in a decision instead of a stopping rule.",
977:   "text": "One asymmetry the design cannot close, and should not hide. Every figure in the replay counts gradings not performed, and a grading is not performed only if some pass declines to perform it. Nothing here makes that happen. A brief emits an id, a proposition, an optional pin and a withheld scope per claim, with no instruction prose in either renderer, and the invariant that keeps every claim in the list is the same one this design refused to touch. The owed section is therefore an artifact a pass may act on, not a mechanism that reduces what it grades. The costs on the other side are unconditional, and the largest of them was missing from an earlier draft: `brief_file` today reads a memo and renders it, calling neither `evidence::load` nor `analyze_ledger` and touching neither the snapshot path nor the workspace identity, so giving it the owed list turns it into a second ledger-analysis driver \u2014 a change of kind, not a threaded parameter. Add the floor through two front ends, a shape change to the JSON brief, and the widenings in the check path. The saving is real only if passes use the list, and no claim here says they will, because nothing in this repository could check it.",
1016:   "text": "This memo designs one change with two halves. `look` decides for itself how much of an observation it returns to the author, and it says what it withheld in two places: in the observation's label, where a later reader of the memo finds it, and in the returned text itself, where the author finds it before writing anything about what they saw. The worktree everything below was read against is pinned: HEAD 81137aa683bdced9bf01a94d34c66b7f4a1758fd on branch tet30-prose-revised-since-proof, with every tracked path unmodified and unstaged and the only entries `git status` reports at all being the eleven untracked files this design itself wrote \u2014 the memo, its evidence sidecar and its snapshot directory. So a reader can re-run any of it against the same tracked bytes. Which of those states each individual fact was captured in is not asserted here: tetel records it with the fact and `check` reports it.",
1029:   "text": "`look_grep` already does the two jobs separately. It runs grep once, then builds `printed` \u2014 the string handed back to the author, which today is grep's stdout verbatim followed by a parenthesised exclusion note \u2014 and, independently, the pending entries: one `Search` record carrying the root, the pattern and a matched-file count, and one `GrepMatch` record per matched file carrying that file's matched lines. The two are derived from the same stdout but neither reads the other, and that separation is what the bound rests on: out of a bounded call, every entry's captured output, its key and its world-tree markers come back byte-identical to what they are today, so two observations of one root still overlap and a later reader still re-reads the same bytes. What does not stay identical is the extent, the pin and the fact that ships. `facts::mint` copies each entry's label straight into the extent and hashes label, world markers and output into the pin, and this design writes a shortfall segment into the label \u2014 so wherever the bound bites, all three differ from what they would otherwise have been. That is the point and not a cost. It is the same property the exclusion note was given when TET-46 chose to list the skipped memo paths rather than count them, so that two searches withholding different things could not fingerprint alike; a bounded search and a whole one should not fingerprint alike either. What makes f3 cheap, and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope, is narrower than \"nothing changes\": no new record, no second pass over the buffer, nothing read back out of the entries, no signature touched. One number is computed while `printed` is being assembled, and the label is built from that number. The direction matters to whoever implements this \u2014 bound first, label from the bound. An implementer who bounds `printed` and leaves the label alone has rebuilt the silent cut this memo exists to remove.",
1123:   "text": "The other `look` path turns out to have a different answer from the one its shape suggests. `look_path` computes `shown` and uses it twice, but not as one value in one place: `printed` is a string of its own that receives a *copy* of `shown` by borrow, and only afterwards is `shown` moved into the pending entry's `output`. Two independent strings exist between those two points, so a bound applied to `printed` there leaves the captured output, the label, the key, the extent, the pin and the snapshot byte-identical \u2014 the same separation `look_grep` has, in a function that reads at first glance as though it has none. There is therefore no code-shaped reason to leave the plain `look <path>` alone, and no other reason either: a whole-file read that overruns the caller's cap is the same silent cut this design exists to stop. So it is bounded too, on the same terms.",
1175:   "text": "Carrying that mechanism across brings its two preconditions with it. The donor states that a shortfall is not an error, and the same must hold here: hitting the bound returns a successful outcome with a bounded body, not a refusal. The code does not force that, and it is worth being exact about why, because the ordering invites the opposite reading: `printed` is assembled before any pending entry exists and the buffer is saved as the last act before the return, so an implementation that bounded while building `printed` could refuse there and discard nothing. What settles it is the crate's own rule about when to refuse. A refusal is for the case where nothing is left to tell and the remedy is singular \u2014 that is exactly how TET-28's census refusal justifies itself, against a check that stayed human-owed because only a person could tell context from conclusion \u2014 and every refusal in this crate's source is of that kind, a missing input or a forbidden flag combination, never a measurement of a result. A byte budget is not that: the number is a judgement, and an author who trips it has no act that re-runs the census smaller. Refusing would take the census away and name nothing to do instead. The donor also states that its key is the resolved path regardless of the range requested, which is what keeps two differently-sized reads of one file overlapping. That holds at the destination too: the `Search` entry is keyed by its root and each match entry by its file, both from paths alone, so a bounded search and an unbounded one of the same root overlap exactly as two unbounded ones would.",
1235:     "why": "For every valid explicit range, the code formats a range annotation; clamping is only applied when the requested end exceeds the file length.",
1245:      "why": "The author's clause claims that `look --lines` adds a range annotation to the label `only when it had to clamp one`. The evidence in F9 shows the implementation of `look_path`, which handles `look --lines`. The code shows that if a line range is provided (`lines` is `Some((a, b))`), the resulting label is *always* formatted with a range, as in `format!(\"{path} lines {a}-{end}\")`. This happens whether the range was clamped (`b > total`) or not (`b <= total`). The condition for adding an annotation is that the `--lines` flag was used at all, not that clamping was necessary. This contradicts the author's claim."
1358:   "text": "All source observations below were taken against one worktree state: branch `tet30-prose-revised-since-proof` at commit `c821b94`, the commit that shipped TET-30's `prose-revised-since-proof` residue. The pin record at the head of this memo's evidence captured `git status` printing nothing at all. No tracked file was modified afterwards; nothing here was implemented. The tree has since gained exactly three paths, all of them this work's own output and all untracked: the memo, its snapshot, and its evidence ledger.",
1386:      "why": "The author's text states that for 'each non-heading block with a non-empty citation list', the check derives an anchor and a block timestamp. The code shows that after identifying such a block, it filters the citation list to only those claims that are 'in proof'. If this filtering results in an empty list (meaning the block has citations, but none are in proof), the code executes `continue`, skipping the derivation of the anchor and block timestamp for that block. The assertion correctly points out this case, which contradicts the 'for each' in the author's description."
1401:   "text": "The sketch left the event's home open between `prose.jsonl` and a sibling log. The evidence closes it, and not on grounds of taste. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged enum over two variants, and the workspace's line reader turns any single unparseable line into an error over the entire log. A third variant is therefore not a compatible addition: I wrote a scratch workspace whose prose log held one ordinary `Create` followed by one `Ack`, and the build at this pin refused the whole file \u2014 including the `Create` it understood perfectly well. Every older build encountering such a snapshot would lose its ability to read prose at all, which is a far worse outcome than the residue line this design exists to clear. The field-level `#[serde(default)]` precedent already in both variants does not extend to a new variant.",
1414:   "text": "So the event lives in its own append-only log, `acks.jsonl`, and the snapshot manifest gains a tenth entry. Three properties, between them, make the failure direction one-way, and the third is the one I had to be shown twice. The manifest is the first: it is an explicit enumeration precisely so that shipping a new workspace file is a decision rather than an accident, so a build predating the entry never opens the file and prints exactly the listing TET-30 shipped. The second is that the ack log only grows, which holds cheaply here because the file does not exist yet: nothing in the tool today can remove or truncate a file it has never heard of, its only writer will be an appending verb, and no withdrawal verb ships. That was where an earlier draft of this section stopped, and stopping there was wrong. Monotonicity is a property of one workspace's log; the mechanism runs over a snapshot. Nothing binds a memo to the workspace that rendered it \u2014 the flag is free on every invocation \u2014 and the writer skips a file the current workspace lacks rather than removing it. So render a memo once from a workspace holding an acknowledgement, then again from a workspace that never held one \u2014 a rebuilt state directory, a second machine \u2014 and the old ack log survives beside the new prose and claims. That is a superset, not a prefix, and it suppresses a block the true state would list, silently. The third property closes it: the ack records the identity of the workspace that minted it, and suppression requires that identity to match the one the snapshot ships. A log from elsewhere is then void rather than honoured, and the failure returns to over-reporting.",
1455:   "text": "The brief called deletion and annotation both doctrine-compatible, and they are not equally good. Deletion loses a distinction the crate elsewhere insists on keeping: a report from which an acknowledged block has vanished cannot be told from a report on a memo where no post-proof revision ever happened, and this is a tool whose no-rows path exists precisely to say that two states which happen to both be quiet are not the same state. The cost of printing is also already paid \u2014 the entry format carries an author's own reason verbatim today, under `revised because:`, with the source comment insisting it is never paraphrased and calling it the most actionable line the entry has.",
1520:   "text": "Underneath those is the property that makes the rest cheap to reason about: the acknowledgement is a filter applied to the trigger's output, never an input to it. The set of blocks a reader is asked to act on can only shrink, so the design cannot invent a demand. A stale ack and an unmatched ack both simply fail to suppress, which is indistinguishable from no ack at all. A corrupt one is the case I first waved through and should not have. The line reader turns any bad line into an error over the entire log, and the one place this crate swallows that silently \u2014 the prose log at check time \u2014 defends the silence with a premise that does not transfer: that a corrupt prose log has already reddened provenance before the check gets there. Keeping acks out of `render` is precisely what makes that false for this file. So an unreadable acknowledgement log has to redden, joining the existing rule that drift and an unreadable snapshot are machine failures because both are objective contradictions decidable without a human. That is the single point where this design touches the machine partition, and it touches it for corruption of the record rather than for anything an acknowledgement means. It is also worth being clear what the digests do not buy: keying on them does not close TET-30's conceded blind spot for prose that ships alongside a claim revision. It only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.",
1559:   "text": "Because the residue is computed against a snapshot and the snapshot is written by `render --out`, an ack minted after a render is invisible until the next one. That sequencing is not new and it is not this design's to fix: everything the check sees about a workspace it sees through the snapshot. What is this design's to decide is whether the acknowledgement changes the memo's bytes, and it must not \u2014 the determinism of `render` in the workspace alone is what makes a drift finding mean anything. Keeping acks out of the rendered output turns the extra render from an annoyance into a useful signal: it rewrites the snapshot in place and leaves the document byte-identical, so the discharge lands in version control as a change to the record with no change to the argument. That is a true description of what an acknowledgement is.",

119:   "text": "So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the ticket hoped for exists. Two were examined; both fail, and no claim is made that a third could not be found. The sharp one \u2014 a record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for, the exact analogue of `out_of_proof` \u2014 cannot be built, for a structural reason rather than an oversight. `out_of_proof` compares digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded. No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape, and the brief a pass receives is id, proposition and pin. Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind, which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line. The weaker one is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away: `render --out` could append a publication record \u2014 each prose block's text digest, each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it \u2014 and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all. It is rejected on resolution, and the reason is structural too. A log that samples only when the author renders cannot order two events that fall inside one interval, and a grading followed by a prose edit followed by a single render is one interval. On the ticket's own account, that is the shape the finding took. The clock-free formulation would have been silent on it. That is the trade, stated plainly: the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering an interval-sampled log cannot, and pays for it with a bound it prints.",
141:   "text": "The last open question asks whether this is a line or a section, and the answer is neither exactly: it is bullets in the flat human-owed list, one per listed block, with a single preamble bullet ahead of them. There are no sub-headings in that partition today, so a section would be the only one and would announce by its shape that it outranks everything beside it. The preamble carries the one thing constant across the entries \u2014 that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same \u2014 and it is printed once rather than per bullet for the reason this crate already recorded when it collapsed `no scope declared` to a single document-level line: repeating a constant per row buries the findings that are actually about the document. Each entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because a block's id is never written into the rendered output and an id alone points at something the reader cannot find; that mapping comes from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render`, so the block-to-line correspondence is described once. The entry then names each cited claim with its first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp \u2014 the inputs to the comparison, printed so a reader can disagree with the conclusion rather than having to trust it.",
174:   "text": "One measurement made in passing deserves recording, because the next ticket in this family will meet it.
