Whole-worktree census of the symbol `NON_COVERAGE`, rooted at /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel — the TET-28 census behind this design's second declared modification target.

The same thing happened as with the `look_grep` census, at a larger size: the search succeeded and was recorded server-side, and the harness refused to return the result, reporting "result (856,178 characters across 87 lines) exceeds maximum allowed tokens" and spilling it to a file. The author again did not read the output of a census they minted. This is the second independent occurrence in this run, so the truncation is the client's standing behaviour on a whole-worktree census of this repository rather than a one-off.

src/observe.rs lines 86-105, the head of `look_path`. It takes a single `path`, refuses if the path does not exist, refuses if the path is a directory (with the message "`tetel look` opens files. Use `tetel look --grep <pattern> {path}` to search it."), and otherwise reads exactly that one file with `fs::read_to_string`. There is no traversal of any kind in this function: it opens the file the caller named and nothing else. So every file `look_path` can ever return is a file the caller named explicitly.

src/observe.rs lines 302-330, `run_command` and its doc comment. It refuses only an empty argv, then spawns `Command::new(&argv[0]).args(&argv[1..])` directly — the doc comment says "executes `argv` directly (never through a shell)". Nothing between the refusal and the spawn inspects, parses or classifies what the command is or what paths it will touch; the entry it records is keyed on `argv.join(" ")`, the command line as a string. So `run` has no place where a path-based exclusion could be applied even in principle, and the bound the ticket states — that the property is about `look` and not about tetel as a whole — is a property of this function's shape rather than a policy choice.

Two consequences of the rule, measured.

(1) A search rooted at docs/design. That directory contains exactly nine entries and every one of them is tetel's own output: three rendered memos, three .evidence.jsonl ledgers, three .tetel snapshot directories. `grep -r -I -n -H -e census <abs docs/design>` returns 184 lines / 1,200,881 bytes; the same search with `--exclude-dir='*.tetel' --exclude='*.evidence.jsonl'` plus one path-spelled `--exclude` per memo returns nothing and exits 1.

(2) Non-stationarity under the rule, on a scratch tree with src/a.rs containing "fn widget() {}", docs/m1.md and docs/m1.md.tetel/facts.jsonl each containing "widget". Pass 1 emitted one rendered-memo exclusion (.../docs/m1.md) and matched `src/a.rs:1:fn widget() {}`. A second memo (docs/m2.md plus docs/m2.md.tetel/) was then added, changing nothing in src/. Pass 2 emitted two rendered-memo exclusions (m1.md and m2.md) and matched exactly the same single line. Compared directly: the matched output was IDENTICAL between the two passes, and the emitted exclusion list was DIFFERENT.

src/facts.rs lines 1-12, the module doc for `tetel fact`. It states that a revision "rewrites the note only, append-only: extent, output and pin are set once at mint time and never appear in a revision event at all, so there is no code path that could change them later either." This is the immutability an answer to "what happens to memos already committed" turns on: a fact minted under the old grep behaviour keeps the extent, output and pin it was minted with, and no later build can rewrite them.

## ## The anchor: first proof, not last pass

The ticket's phrase "the last grounding pass" is not merely ambiguous, as its own open questions suspected — read literally it is self-defeating, and this is the design's first and largest departure. Every grounding pass is briefed on every claim in the ledger, whether or not it has been graded before, so a pass that finds nothing to change still appends a fresh record against the unchanged wording. The two memos already in this tree show what that produces: one claim carrying ten records on a single unchanged digest, written by three passes across nearly half an hour, and another graded `qualifies` twice by different passes a quarter of an hour apart on text nobody touched. Anchor the comparison at the most recent grading and the anchor walks forward every round; fix-round prose written in round three stops being "since the last pass" the moment round four runs, even though no pass has ever read a word of the prose. On the ticket's own account of it, the trail this residue is named after ran six rounds. So the anchor is the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof. A later pass over unchanged text cannot move it, and only a revision of the claim itself, followed by a grading of the new wording, ever does.

*cites: C3*

## ## The rule

With the anchor fixed, the rule almost states itself, and the places where it does not are the places attack put there. A prose block is listed when it is a paragraph rather than a heading, it cites at least one id, at least one cited id resolves to a ledger claim that is in proof, and the block's text timestamp is later than the latest first proof among those in-proof citations. "In proof" is not a new predicate: it is the digest comparison `analyze_ledger` already performs, empty-digest grandfathering included. The block's text timestamp is the earliest event in its history whose text and citation list both equal the current ones. Neither half of that definition was in the first draft of this design and neither is decoration — the next two sections are about what each one closes. The two quantifier choices the ticket left open fall out of the anchor rather than being decided by taste. Per claim, take the earliest in-proof record, because that is when the wording settled. Per block, take the latest of those, because a block is not anchored until its evidence base has settled — taking the earliest instead would list every paragraph whose text merely postdates its first-graded citation, which is nearly all of them. Both memos already in this tree list nothing, and that includes the two real post-pass prose revisions they contain between them, tet29's P4 and tet28's P18. Each was rewritten in a fix round after a pass had run, and each is correctly silent for the same reason: each also cites a claim revised in that same round, whose new wording entered proof only afterwards. The maximum is doing exactly the work it was chosen for. That also means the listing behaviour had to be tested on constructions appended to those logs rather than on a real defect: move a tet29 paragraph past its claim's first proof and touch no claim, and it is listed alone.

*cites: C4*

On the ticket's first open question — creation or revision — the residue is about neither act specifically but about the text's age: the timestamp is derived from the block's events without caring whether the earliest one bearing its current wording was a creation or a rewrite. The exposure is the same in both directions, since a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one, and the ticket's own vector could have arrived either way. Counting creations also cannot inflate the list through paragraphs added to carry a new assertion under a new claim, and the reason is mechanical rather than statistical: a claim not yet in proof cannot anchor a block at all, and once a pass has put it in proof that first proof necessarily postdates a paragraph written before the pass ran. How often a fix-round paragraph takes that shape rather than resting on old claims is a question about how authors behave, and nothing here measures it. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, settled claims.
## No opt-out, and what "explicitly named" costs

There should be no `--include-tetel`. The honest escape hatch already exists three times over, and each time it is reached by naming something rather than by setting a flag: open the file with `look <path>`, search with a tetel path as the root, or use `run`. The second of those is not a concession this design makes but a constraint it is under, since grep suppresses a directory named as the recursion root when `--exclude-dir` matches it, so the flags have to be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would return nothing at all. The third is the hole the ticket already states and cannot be closed: `run` spawns its argv directly with nothing between the empty-argument refusal and the spawn that inspects the command or the paths it will touch, so there is no place an exclusion could be applied even in principle. A flag would add a fourth route with a property none of these has — it leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call.

*cites: C16*

The hard case the ticket asked about is a root like `docs/design`, which in this repository contains nine entries and not one of them is anything but tetel's own output. Under this rule it is not explicitly named — it is an ordinary directory whose path says nothing about tetel — so the exclusions apply and a search rooted there returns nothing at all where today it returns 1,200,881 bytes. That is a real loss and it is accepted deliberately, because the alternative is to decide that a directory counts as named when everything under it happens to be tetel's, which is a judgement about contents rather than a test on a path, and this project does not let a refusal make judgements. The price is one extra keystroke of specificity: to search across memos, name a memo or a snapshot, not the folder they live in.

Stop when `check` is machine-clean and no live claim is refuted or unexplained. Report then.

**Human-owed items never clear and are not failures.** `check` will always list qualified verdicts,
`proc:` extents, self-grounding, and its own standing non-coverage. Machine-checked clean is the
bar; the human-owed partition is what you hand the reader, not a queue to empty. Surviving
qualifications belong in your report with the grounder's own words.

**Stop after the first round that provokes no revision. Do not run a second.** Measured across all
four memos: the final grading pass provoked **zero** claim revisions every time. So the last round is
never free — it is what tells you the design has settled, and it is worth paying once. One memo paid
twice: two consecutive dry rounds, 55 records between them, nothing changed by either. The second was
waste under any stop rule. A round that changes nothing has done its job; a second one has not. This
is the floor; the cap below is the ceiling, and a run should hit whichever comes first.

**Cap yourself at four grounding rounds.** If you are still not clean, stop and say so plainly:
which claims will not survive, what each pass said, and what you believe the design cannot currently
establish. An honest report of an unstable design is a result. A design reported as finished because
the loop ran out of patience is not — and it is worse than the unstable one, because it arrives with
a green attached.

Two observations on the pin operands.

(1) src/facts.rs lines 400-455: a fact's `pin` is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` where hash_input concatenates, for every pending entry, its label, world_root, world_state and output. The comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker", folding the marker in so "a fact minted against a different tree state pins differently even if its labels/output happen to coincide" — and notes the marker "is still carried separately in `extent`". So a fact pin is a hash of the observation's content, not a tree identifier: two facts minted in one checkout at one commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ.

(2) Running the installed tetel binary as `brief --json` over all five rendered memos in docs/design (tet28, tet29, tet30, tet46, tet47): 15, 14, 13, 19 and 26 claims respectively — 87 in total — and ZERO carry a `pin` in any of them. `render_json` omits the field when `Claim::pin` is None, so `find_stated_pin` yields None for every claim in every memo this project has written, including this one.

Two observations on where a tree state is and is not available.

(1) src/evidence.rs lines 548-600, the record read-back. `EvidenceRecord` is constructed from the statement with claim_id, verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, note, pin, timestamp, witnessed and proposition_digest — the predicate's `world: Vec<Marker>` field is NOT read back. So the tree markers a witnessed record carries are written into the evidence JSONL and dropped when it is loaded for `check`.

A world-state marker is `git:<sha256 of "rev-parse HEAD" NUL "git diff HEAD --binary">` — "which together determine every tracked file's content: `HEAD` names the base, the diff names the delta from it". No test asserts the list's length or its exact membership at any of these sites, so adding an entry is a one-line edit at the definition. Same exclusions applied as the other censuses in this memo.

The "nothing derived is stored" doctrine, as stated in src/lib.rs:136-141: the tree-state report is read "from the same shipped `facts.jsonl`; nothing derived is stored, and a re-run recomputes it." The rule is scoped to values a later re-run can recompute from the shipped ledger — it is stated as a reason for recomputing rather than persisting, not as a prohibition on recording what happened.

Contrary to the reading that return and capture are one value in `look_path`: at src/observe.rs:314-330 `printed` is a distinct `String::new()` that receives a COPY of `shown` via `printed.push_str(&shown)` (a borrow), and only afterwards is `shown` MOVED into `PendingEntry { output: shown, .. }`. Between the push_str and the move there are two independent strings, so a bound applied to `printed` at that point cannot reach `entry.output`, the entry's `label`, its `key`, its `world_root`/`world_state`, or anything that ships into the snapshot. Whatever `look_path` captures is byte-identical whether or not `printed` was bounded. The `label` computed at 297-312 is likewise built from `contents`/`lines`, never from `printed`.

The crate does truncate author-supplied text in one place today, and it has a spelling for it. `refuse_incomplete` (src/transplants.rs:420-443) shortens each undischarged premise for its refusal message: `let first = text.lines().next().unwrap_or("").trim();` then `let shown = if text.lines().count() > 1 { format!("{first} …") } else { first.to_string() };`. Two properties are legible from those two lines: the cut is taken at a LINE boundary (`lines().next()`, never a byte or character offset), and the shortened text carries a trailing marker — a space followed by U+2026 — applied when and only when something was actually removed, so an untruncated premise gains no marker at all. What the spelling does NOT carry is any measure of how much was withheld: neither the count of lines dropped nor any total appears in `shown` or in `msg`. This is a marker in the returned text itself, not in any label or record.

What an author actually sees at capture time, on both front ends. The CLI (src/main.rs:506-510) does `print!("{}", outcome.printed)` on success and nothing else; the MCP handler (src/mcp.rs:643-646) does `text_result(outcome.printed)` on success and nothing else. Neither returns the observation's label, its key, or any other field of the pending entry — `printed` is the whole of what `look` hands back. The label first becomes visible to the author one act later, inside the `fact` result: `mcp.rs:670-676` loads the pending buffer, builds `folded` via `facts::describe_buffer`, and ships it in `fact_result` — and by that point the note is already a parameter of the same call (`facts::FactRequest::Mint { note: p.note }`, mcp.rs:666), i.e. the assertion over the observation was supplied before the label was ever shown. So anything written only into the label is legible to a later reader of the memo and to the author only after they have committed the note.

text:
Two things about refusing rather than reporting a bound in `look_grep`.

(1) The ordering does NOT force report-over-refuse. In the match branch (src/observe.rs:438-478) `printed.push_str(&stdout)` and the exclusion note run FIRST, before `by_file` is built and before any `PendingEntry` is constructed; the `Search` entry and the per-file `GrepMatch` entries are pushed onto the in-memory `buf` after that, and `pending::save(workspace_dir, &buf)?` is the last statement before `Ok(LookOutcome { printed })`. So an implementation that bounds while assembling `printed` reaches the bound before any entry exists and before anything is persisted, and could return `Err` there discarding nothing. Nothing in this range makes a refusal impossible.

(2) What does decide it is the crate's own report-versus-refuse discriminator, stated in `targets.rs`'s module doc (targets.rs:44-49): the census refusal is a refusal because "Here nothing is left to tell: the remedy is singular. Run the workspace-rooted grep, mint the fact, cite it — or withdraw the target", as against `scope`, which "stayed human-owed because only a person can tell context from conclusion". A whole-`src` grep for `refuse` shows every `workspace::refuse` call site in the crate is of that singular-remedy kind — a missing or malformed input, or a forbidden flag combination: claims.rs (no --proposition, no such claim, --revise without --why, unknown cited fact), facts.rs (empty note, no such fact), prose.rs (--ack combined with any of --text/--revise/--heading/--level/--cites/--before, --level out of 1..=6), targets.rs (no symbol, uncensused symbol), transplants.rs (empty --text, withdrawn ids, an unanswered premise at render), observe.rs (no such path, invalid --lines range, `--grep` without a path, `lines` with `grep`). Not one refusal anywhere in src is keyed to the size or content of a result. A byte budget is not a singular-remedy condition: the author who hits it has no act that re-runs the search under the budget.

| C4 | The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) at least one cited id resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger that is in proof — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of that claim's current proposition, the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses, empty digest grandfathered — and (c) the block's text timestamp is strictly greater than the maximum, over its in-proof cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. A block's text timestamp is the timestamp of the earliest event in its history whose text AND citation list both equal the current ones; for a block never revised it is simply its creation. Both halves of that definition are load-bearing and both were found by attack rather than by design. Keying on the citation list as well as the text is what stops a citation-only revision from moving the anchor while the timestamp stays frozen — an unrefused and indeed encouraged act, since `prose::revise` never compares text and its `cite` parameter exists precisely to let an author add a citation to existing prose. Making clause (b) existential rather than universal is what stops a single record-less citation from suppressing a block silently, and it costs nothing, because a claim with no record has no first proof to enter the maximum. Both shipped memos list nothing as they stand. That includes the two real post-pass prose revisions they contain between them — tet29's P4 at 1786174635 and tet28's P18 at 1786132480, each rewritten in a fix round after a pass had run. Each is correctly not listed for the same reason: each also cites a claim revised in that same fix round, whose new wording entered proof only afterwards, and clause (c) takes the maximum. The listing behaviour was therefore tested on constructions appended to tet29's real logs rather than on a real fix-round rewrite that the rule catches. Given a constructed rewrite of tet29's P11 at a timestamp after its claim's first proof, the rule lists it, and continues to list it under a citation-only revision adding an already-in-proof claim, under one adding a record-less claim, and under the dual where an old uncited paragraph is given a settled citation. | OWED |
| C5 | The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: a block's text timestamp is derived from its prose events without regard to whether the earliest event bearing its current text was a `Create` or a `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp`. Including creations closes an identical exposure, because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It also cannot inflate the listing by way of paragraphs written to carry a new assertion under a new claim: a claim not yet in proof cannot anchor a block at all, and once some pass has put it in proof that first proof postdates a paragraph written before the pass ran — under the same-clock assumption C7 states this design cannot establish, since the two timestamps come from different processes — so such a block is not listable either way. How often a fix-round paragraph takes that shape rather than resting on old claims is a question about authoring behaviour that nothing here measures. What creation-counting does catch is a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims. | OWED |
| C6 | The anchor and the pair gate together make a listing unclearable by anything that did not either restore the settled text or move the evidence. A further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block. A citation-only revision cannot silence one either: it changes the citation set, so the block's text timestamp moves to that revision, and pointing a paragraph at a claim already in proof therefore lists it rather than clearing it. Nor can adding a record-less citation, since the in-proof test is existential and an ungrounded claim contributes no first proof. Two things clear a listing. Reverting the text and citations to what they were when the claims settled, which works because the timestamp is looked up by content rather than by event order even though prose.jsonl is append-only. And revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, which is the remedy the finding calls for, since the defect is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost, stated rather than hidden: neither remedy is cheap, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until some claim moves or the edit is undone, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line. Nothing in the rule bounds how many blocks that can reach — an author who flow-edits every paragraph of a settled memo will see every paragraph listed, and on a memo like tet29, whose twelve blocks are all cited paragraphs with no headings among them, that is all twelve. So this is not distinguished from the `no scope declared` line that once printed once per claim by being structurally small. | C7 | This is the first check to compare an authoring workspace's clock against a grounding pass's, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large. | OWED |
| C8 | Two digest-shaped alternatives were examined and both fail, though this is not a claim that no third exists. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost, and the reason is a property of any interval-sampled log rather than of any particular incident: such a log records state only at the moments the author chooses to render, so two events falling inside one interval cannot be ordered against each other at all. A grading followed by a prose edit followed by a single render is exactly one such interval, and the residue would be silent on it. | C10 | The residue is bullets in the existing flat human-owed list, not a new section, and it is identified by document line as well as by block id. And revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, which is the remedy the finding calls for". It then states the cost verbatim: "neither remedy is cheap, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until some claim moves or the edit is undone, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line." C6 also establishes that a further grounding pass over unchanged wording "appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block", and that a citation-only revision lists rather than clears.

C11 states the guarantee this design breaks, verbatim: "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes, nothing is executed and no file the document names is opened." C11 also states "`machine_check_failed` is not touched, which is what makes this human-owed by construction rather than by intention", and that the check's claims must come from the rendered document's imported ledger, never the snapshot's claims.jsonl, because the two sources are not the same string.

C5 states creations count as well as revisions, and closes the evasion whereby a fresh paragraph under already-settled claims would otherwise escape.

In src/checks.rs, `Findings::machine_check_failed` returns true if any of grammar_errors, subset_failures, abutting_failures, unsettled_failures, cascade_failures, ledger_errors, verdict_disagreements, out_of_proof, uncensused_targets, unquoted_premises is non-empty, or `provenance_failed()`. `prose_revised_since_proof` is declared on `Findings` immediately above this impl and is NOT among them. text: An authoring workspace directory (listing `~/.local/state/tetel/workspaces/tet30`) contains exactly: claims.jsonl, counters.json, facts.jsonl, identity.json, pending.json, prose.jsonl, targets.jsonl. There is no evidence file of any kind in it. Evidence records live beside the rendered memo instead: `docs/design/` holds, for each of the five committed memos, `<name>.md`, `<name>.md.evidence.jsonl` and `<name>.md.tetel/`. So an authoring workspace has no access to grounding records, and therefore cannot compute a claim's first proof or a block's anchor at mint time.

The render/snapshot sequencing. In src/main.rs (lines 838-882), `render --out` writes the rendered document with `std::fs::write(&path, &rendered)` FIRST, then calls `snapshot::write(&path, &workspace_dir)`, with the comment "Document first, then snapshot: if the snapshot write fails the document still exists and `check` reports the missing record, which is a recoverable state. The third and last entry in the whole constant is the block-total one: "a citation whose claim settled before the block's wording, when another citation in the same block settled after it — the anchor is the latest first proof among all of a block's citations, so the earlier-settled one is never compared against the wording on its own; a co-cited claim that keeps being revised and re-entering proof keeps raising the anchor, and whether the wording was ever actually examined against the earlier-settled claim is never answered by any listing here". Every string in the constant is static; the comment in the head group states "This can only ever be the general statement — every string in this list is static and none is per-search".

Two things my implementation-surface and degradation-direction claims got wrong.

(1) THE SHARED FRONT-END SHAPE IS ITSELF A SURFACE. src/prose.rs lines 205-275: `ProseRequest` is a three-variant enum (`Revise { id, text, why, cite }`, `Heading { text, level, before }`, `Paragraph { text, cite, before }`); `ProseOutcome` is a two-variant enum (`Revised { id }`, `Created(Block)`); and `dispatch` consumes the request in an EXHAUSTIVE `match req { ... }` over all three variants. So adding an ack mode is not confined to a new module: it adds a variant to `ProseRequest`, an arm to `dispatch`'s match, and — since an acknowledgement is neither `Revised` nor `Created` — a variant to `ProseOutcome`, which each front end matches on. The doc comment's own reason for the shared shape is "so the two front ends can never drift on which combination of missing flags gets refused, or with what text", i.e. the shape exists precisely because per-front-end mode chains drift.

(2) `snapshot::write` COPIES AND NEVER REMOVES. src/snapshot.rs lines 133-155: the body is `for name in SNAPSHOT_FILES { let src = workspace_dir.join(name); if src.exists() { fs::copy(&src, dir.join(name))?; } }`. There is no deletion and no reconciliation: a file present in the snapshot but absent from the workspace is left in place, and a file the running build's `SNAPSHOT_FILES` does not name is never touched at all. So a snapshot's copy of any given log is not necessarily the workspace's log as of the last render — it is the most recent copy any build ever made of it.

A search of src/ for `mod tests {` returns 15 lines: brief.rs:225, ledger.rs:354, review.rs:152, checks.rs:1482, buildid.rs:216, compose.rs:366, worldstate.rs:294, citations.rs:338, report.rs:497, scope.rs:425 (plus `pub(crate) mod tests_support {` at scope.rs:397), evidence.rs:576, snapshot.rs:210, workspace.rs:477, observe.rs:624.

Four of the five files holding `fs::remove` sites appear here with a test module opening ABOVE every one of their remove lines: review.rs (152 < 165), evidence.rs (576 < 612-750), workspace.rs (477 < 522-561), observe.rs (624 < 636-672). facts.rs does NOT appear in this list at all, so this search does not locate its test module and establishes nothing about whether facts.rs:559-601 sit inside one.

Two earlier searches in the same tree for `#\[cfg\(test\)\]` and for `cfg\(test\)` both returned NO MATCHES, which given that in-file test modules plainly exist means this tool's grep did not interpret those patterns as I intended rather than that the attribute is absent. I record the negative results as uninformative, not as evidence the attribute does not appear.

Nothing binds a rendered memo to the workspace that produced it. src/main.rs lines 820-842: the render arm is `Command::Render { out } => { let workspace_dir = tetel::workspace::workspace_dir(&cli.workspace); ... }` — the workspace comes from the global `--workspace` flag on each invocation, and the destination comes from `out`. There is no lookup of who rendered this path before, no comparison against anything in an existing `<memo>.tetel/`, and no refusal on a mismatch. So `tetel --workspace W1 render --out M` followed later by `tetel --workspace W2 render --out M` is an ordinary, unrefused sequence.

Combined with `snapshot::write`'s copy loop (recorded separately: it copies only `if src.exists()` and never removes), this means the snapshot beside M after the second render holds W2's prose.jsonl, claims.jsonl and identity.json alongside any file W2 does not have that W1 previously wrote — those are left in place untouched. The snapshot's contents are therefore not necessarily the contents of any single workspace.
